question: When ChatGPT writes a reply, it does not type words — it predicts small pieces called tokens. A token might be a whole word, a syllable, or even a single letter. This means the model:

question: Asked 'what is 78,453 × 91,824?' an LLM without a calculator tool will usually:

choices: Produce a confident, plausibly-formatted number that is wrong

context: LLMs predict the next token, not the next digit of an arithmetic result. Big multiplications are pattern-matched, not calculated. Modern products work around this by handing math to an actual calculator tool — but the raw model is still bad at it.

question: Close a chat, open a new one, ask the same model 'what did we talk about yesterday?' By default, the answer will be that it does not know. Why?

context: An LLM holds context only within a single conversation window. Some products bolt on memory tools (saved notes, retrieval databases). The model itself does not remember — it is the application layer that decides what to feed back in.

question: An LLM is given a string of text and asked to produce the next bit. At the lowest level, the model is doing one thing:
answer: Predicting which token is most likely to come next, given the ones so far
choices: Predicting which token is most likely to come next, given the ones so far
Looking up the right answer in a stored knowledge base of facts
Reasoning step by step through a chain of formal logical rules
Searching the live web for the best response to the prompt given
context: Next-token prediction is the whole engine. Everything that looks like conversation, reasoning, or creativity emerges from a model very good at picking the next chunk. This is humbling — and a clue to where the cracks show.

question: An LLM is sometimes called 'deep' — referring to a feature of its neural network design:

context: Deep learning = neural networks with many hidden layers between input and output. 'Depth' is a literal architectural feature, not a metaphor for insight. Image-recognition CNNs may have 50+ layers; transformers stack 100+ attention blocks.

question: A model produces a confident, well-formatted citation to a real-sounding research paper. You look the paper up — it does not exist. The term for this kind of failure is:
answer: Hallucination
choices: Hallucination

Caching error
context: Hallucination is the canonical failure mode of generative AI: confident, plausible, false. The model predicts what a citation usually looks like — and you get a paper that should exist but does not. Always verify dates, authors, and sources yourself.

question: An LLM does not 'know' anything in the way a person does. It is more accurate to say the model has learned:
answer: Statistical patterns over enormous amounts of text it was trained on
choices: Statistical patterns over enormous amounts of text it was trained on
Conscious understanding of concepts, similar to a human reader
A hidden knowledge graph built by human editors in advance
The truth values of every statement in its training data
context: An LLM is not a database, and it is not a mind. It is a giant statistical model of which token tends to follow which. Calling it 'understanding' is convenient shorthand; treating it like real understanding gets you in trouble.

question: A chatbot's reply length is limited by something called the context window. Roughly, this is:
answer: The maximum number of tokens the model can read and write in one exchange
choices: The maximum number of tokens the model can read and write in one exchange
The number of seconds the user can wait before the screen times out
The number of users the model can serve at once on a single server
The number of full conversations the model keeps in long-term memory
context: Context window = working memory. Early GPT-3 was about 2K tokens; modern frontier models reach 200K to 2M tokens. Past the window, the model has to drop earlier content — and may quietly forget what was said.

question: A chatbot is given a setting called temperature, ranging from 0 upward. Set to 0, the model:
answer: Picks the single most likely next token every time — output is the most predictable
choices: Picks the single most likely next token every time — output is the most predictable
Generates only short, terse answers that strip out details and softeners
Refuses to answer politically charged or otherwise sensitive prompts
Returns the literal training-data text most similar to the question
context: Temperature controls randomness in token selection. Zero is deterministic and dry; higher values inject creativity at the cost of consistency. Set too high, the model wanders into nonsense; set too low, it sounds like a tired official.

question: The 'attention' mechanism at the heart of a transformer model is doing roughly this for each word it produces:
answer: Weighing how much each earlier token in the input matters to the one being produced
choices: Weighing how much each earlier token in the input matters to the one being produced
Focusing the user's eyes on the most important part of the answer
Allocating GPU memory among competing reasoning sub-tasks
Watching the user's input for keywords that trigger safety filters
context: Self-attention is the engine of the transformer. For each new token, the model computes a weighted sum over earlier tokens — paying 'attention' to what matters now. It is mathematical, not perceptual; the metaphor 'attention' is a name, not a claim.

question: An LLM is asked, 'browse the web and tell me today's news.' On its own, without tools, the model:
answer: Cannot — its weights are frozen; only a wrapper with a search tool can fetch live data
choices: Cannot — its weights are frozen; only a wrapper with a search tool can fetch live data
Quietly pulls down today's pages from a cached copy of the web in its weights
Asks the operating system for permission to open a browser session
Updates its training data nightly and reads off the latest stored version
context: An LLM is not a search engine. Modern products bolt on tools — Bing, Google, custom retrieval — and route queries to them. Without that pipeline, the model is a closed book and will hallucinate confidently if pushed.

question: Asked to write a Python function, a modern LLM looks like a coder. Underneath the hood, what is it doing?
answer: Predicting the next token, drawing on many code examples seen during training
choices: Predicting the next token, drawing on many code examples seen during training
Running a logical proof to ensure the code is mathematically correct
Executing the code in a sandbox before showing it to the user
Looking the function up in a database of solved coding problems
context: Code is text. LLMs trained on GitHub plus documentation are very good at producing plausible code, including subtle bugs. Compilers and tests catch what models miss. Treat AI-generated code like a colleague's draft — read it before you trust it.

question: Two AI systems that play chess or Go — one a 'narrow' game engine, the other a general chatbot — differ most clearly in:
answer: Range of tasks: the engine plays one game well; the chatbot does many things, none perfectly
choices: Range of tasks: the engine plays one game well; the chatbot does many things, none perfectly

Programming language: chess engines use C, chatbots use English internally
Consciousness: chess engines are aware while chatbots merely simulate it
context: 'AGI' versus 'narrow AI' is the old framing: Stockfish is godlike at chess and nothing else; a chatbot is mediocre at chess but also writes poems. Frontier LLMs are broad but still narrow versus a person — and not conscious in either case.

question: An LLM produces a long, confident answer in academic-sounding English. What does the eloquence tell you about whether the content is true?
answer: Nothing — fluency is independent of accuracy in an LLM's output
choices: Nothing — fluency is independent of accuracy in an LLM's output

It is likely false — confident answers should always be doubted

context: An LLM learned to sound like a textbook by reading textbooks. It learned what true sentences look like; it did not learn how to check. Confidence and correctness are decoupled. Always verify facts, even the well-written ones.

question: A model trained on internet text picks up the biases and gaps of that text. This is sometimes called:
answer: Training-data bias — the model reflects what was in its inputs
choices: Training-data bias — the model reflects what was in its inputs

Architectural bias — caused by the choice of transformer layers
Compiler bias — added when the code is translated for the GPU
context: If your training data over-represents one viewpoint, time, or language, the model leans that way. Fine-tuning and RLHF then add a second layer of bias from human reviewers and their instructions. Both are real; both are worth naming.

question: A user types a long message into a chatbot that has a 100,000-token context window. As the conversation goes on, eventually the model starts forgetting earlier details. Why?
answer: Older content slides out of the window once total tokens exceed the limit
choices: Older content slides out of the window once total tokens exceed the limit

The model's attention is randomly disabled to save energy in long chats
context: When the conversation is longer than the window, the application has to trim. Older messages get dropped, summarized, or moved to a retrieval database. To the model, anything outside the window does not exist.

question: An LLM is asked to translate a sentence from French to English. It does well because:
answer: Its training data included enormous amounts of parallel French and English text
choices: Its training data included enormous amounts of parallel French and English text
It has a built-in French-English dictionary lookup module inside it
It speaks French and English as a bilingual human would speak them
It uses Google Translate as a tool every time it produces a sentence
context: LLMs are stunningly good at translation for major languages — without being designed for translation. The reason is unglamorous: the internet has tons of parallel text, and pattern-completion at scale catches the regularities of translation as a side effect.

question: A model is described as 'open weights.' What does that mean for someone who wants to use it?

The model is free to use but only via the original vendor's website

question: An LLM's 'reasoning' often improves when you ask it to 'show its work' step by step. This technique is called:
answer: Chain-of-thought prompting
choices: Chain-of-thought prompting
Symbolic logic injection
Recursive descent parsing
Forward-pass debugging
context: Asking the model to explain its steps gives it more tokens to compute over, and the resulting chain often catches errors the one-shot answer would not. It is a hack of the next-token machinery — but a useful one. Newer 'reasoning' models do this automatically.

question: Training a giant model from scratch costs millions in compute. A common practical alternative is:
answer: Transfer learning — start from a pretrained model and adapt it to your task
choices: Transfer learning — start from a pretrained model and adapt it to your task
Brute search — try every weight assignment until the loss drops
Genetic mutation — randomly tweak weights and keep the survivors
Manual coding — write the desired behavior in plain conditionals
context: Transfer learning is the workhorse of practical AI. A foundation model trained on enormous general data is fine-tuned on a small task-specific dataset. Hours instead of months; thousands of dollars instead of millions. Almost every applied project starts here.

question: A 'foundation model' refers to:
answer: A large pretrained model that many specific applications are built on top of
choices: A large pretrained model that many specific applications are built on top of
The first version of any AI model released to the public for free
The hardware layer beneath all neural-network training and inference
An open-source model that is required by EU AI Act regulations
context: Foundation model = the shared base everyone else builds on. GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, Llama are foundation models. Specialized assistants, search products, and developer tools are built by fine-tuning or prompting them. The shape of the AI economy.

question: A model whose training data was scraped from the open web inherits which property by default?
answer: The viewpoints, gaps, and quality variance of whatever was on the internet
choices: The viewpoints, gaps, and quality variance of whatever was on the internet
Strict neutrality, because the web averages all viewpoints out fairly
Perfect factual recall, because the web contains all human knowledge
The opinions of the model's developers, hardcoded into its weights
context: Garbage in, garbage out. The web is not neutral — Reddit, Wikipedia, news media, and academic papers all dominate, each with their own tilts. A model trained on this corpus inherits its center of mass, which is not the same as humanity's center of mass.

question: A model card or system card published with a new LLM typically describes:
answer: Training data approximations, intended uses, known limitations, and safety evaluations
choices: Training data approximations, intended uses, known limitations, and safety evaluations
The exact training data, line by line, in a publicly searchable file
The IQ of the model on standardized tests against human controls
The model's political opinions on currently contested public issues
context: Model cards are a transparency norm that became standard around 2019 onward. They rarely show full training data — that is treated as a trade secret — but they should describe risks, gaps, and evaluation results. Worth reading.

question: When a model is asked the same question twice and gives two different answers, the reason is usually:
answer: Randomness in token sampling — controlled by the temperature setting
choices: Randomness in token sampling — controlled by the temperature setting
The model is intentionally trying to confuse the user
The model has a different opinion each day depending on its mood
Different users get different answers based on their account history
context: At temperature greater than zero, the model samples from a distribution over tokens — so the same prompt yields different outputs. Set temperature to zero and you usually get the same answer every time. The variability is mathematical, not psychological.

question: A model is described as 'multimodal.' This means it can:
answer: Handle more than one kind of input — for example, text and images together
choices: Handle more than one kind of input — for example, text and images together
Run in multiple modes — fast or accurate, but never both at once
Switch its language between English, Spanish, and Mandarin Chinese
Operate without a graphics card by switching to CPU mode at runtime
context: Multimodal models accept text, images, audio, sometimes video. GPT-4V, Claude 3, Gemini, Llama Vision — all multimodal in some sense. Internally everything still becomes embeddings; the modalities are unified in the vector space.

question: A model passes one full sweep over the entire training dataset. That sweep is called:
answer: An epoch
choices: An epoch
A batch
A step
A run
context: Training proceeds in batches; many batches make an epoch; many epochs make a training run. Frontier LLMs sometimes train on a dataset for less than one full epoch, because the dataset is so enormous and overfitting is the bigger risk.

question: An LLM is told 'write a story.' Two seconds later it starts producing words at a steady pace. Internally, what is happening?
answer: It generates one token at a time, each conditioned on everything produced so far
choices: It generates one token at a time, each conditioned on everything produced so far
It writes the entire story silently first, then types it out to the user
It picks one of several pre-written stories matching the prompt's keywords
It runs a planning algorithm to outline first, then fills in each section
context: Generation is sequential: pick next token, append, pick next, append. The illusion of 'thinking ahead' comes from training on enough text that local predictions look globally coherent. There is no plan inside; only one token at a time.

question: A 'Mixture of Experts' model means:
answer: The model contains many specialized sub-networks; only some run for each input
choices: The model contains many specialized sub-networks; only some run for each input
Several different models vote on each answer and pick the majority view
Real human experts review every answer the model gives before delivery
The model was trained by combining many specialized experts in a panel
context: MoE: instead of one giant dense network, many smaller experts plus a router. The router picks a few experts per token; only those run. You get the capacity of a huge model with the cost of a smaller one. Mixtral and DeepSeek made it popular.

question: A modern LLM with a 100K-token context window can hold roughly:
answer: About 75,000 English words — a short novel — in working memory at once
choices: About 75,000 English words — a short novel — in working memory at once
About 10,000 English words — a long essay — in working memory at once
About 500 English words — a short article — in working memory at once
Effectively unlimited text — the window is a soft limit, not a hard one
context: Rough rule of thumb: one token is about three-quarters of a word in English. A 100K-token window is enough for an entire short book. Frontier models in 2024-2025 reach 1M to 2M tokens — a whole shelf of books in one prompt.

question: Two models, same size, trained on different data, will:
answer: Show different strengths, weaknesses, biases, and styles
choices: Show different strengths, weaknesses, biases, and styles
Behave identically — model size is what determines all behavior
Be detectable as different only by the model's developers, not users
Have the same answers; differences are in the user interface only
context: Training data is destiny. Two transformers with the same architecture but different data will have different vocabularies, different gaps, and different biases. The architecture matters less than the recipe of what you feed it.

question: The 'training' phase of a frontier LLM typically lasts:
answer: Weeks to months, using thousands of GPUs running in parallel
choices: Weeks to months, using thousands of GPUs running in parallel
A few hours on a single desktop computer with a normal graphics card
Decades of continuous learning to absorb all human knowledge slowly
Less than one minute — the slow part is the front-end design instead
context: Training GPT-class models is an industrial operation: thousands of NVIDIA H100s, months of wall-clock time, electricity bills in the millions. This is why frontier model training is concentrated in a handful of well-funded companies.

question: Compared to a search engine like Google, a chatbot LLM is better at:
answer: Synthesizing and explaining; worse at fresh facts and citing sources
choices: Synthesizing and explaining; worse at fresh facts and citing sources
Every task, with no notable weaknesses against search engines
Citing sources; worse at fluent prose and explanation of concepts
Returning a single right document; worse at extended discussion
context: Use the right tool. Google is faster at 'what is happening right now,' 'what does this exact site say,' or 'where did this come from.' A chatbot is faster at 'explain this concept,' 'draft me a letter,' or 'summarize this argument.'

question: An LLM 'thinks' in the sense that it computes with statistics over text. To say it 'thinks' the way a person does is:
answer: A loose metaphor — the model does not have beliefs, intent, or self-awareness
choices: A loose metaphor — the model does not have beliefs, intent, or self-awareness
A scientific claim that most AI researchers now accept as proven
Provably false — only humans can be said to think at all
Strictly true — models think more clearly than most people do
context: Be careful with thinking, knowing, wanting, feeling when applied to an LLM. The words borrow the texture of mind while describing arithmetic. Useful shorthand in conversation; misleading if taken literally. Capability is not consciousness.

question: A new model is described as having '70 billion parameters.' The size tells you most about:
answer: Its capacity to hold patterns; not directly its intelligence or factual accuracy
choices: Its capacity to hold patterns; not directly its intelligence or factual accuracy
Its IQ on standardized human tests, on a roughly linear scale
Its training cost, exactly proportional to the parameter count alone
Its accuracy on factual questions, with bigger always being better
context: Bigger models can store more, but data quality, training method, and fine-tuning matter at least as much. A smaller, better-trained model often beats a bigger, sloppier one. Parameter count is one number among several — not a single quality score.

question: Image-generation models like Stable Diffusion and DALL-E work by:
answer: Gradually denoising random patterns into an image guided by a text prompt
choices: Gradually denoising random patterns into an image guided by a text prompt
Pasting together small fragments from real photographs in their training set
Drawing line by line, the way a human illustrator builds up a sketch
Asking a separate LLM to describe the image and then rendering it directly
context: Diffusion models start from pure noise and run many steps of denoising, each step nudging the image toward what the prompt describes. It is closer to chiseling away marble than to painting. Each output is fresh, not a collage of training images.

question: Asked 'what is the date today?' a vanilla LLM with no tools will:
answer: Guess based on its training cutoff — often a year or more in the past
choices: Guess based on its training cutoff — often a year or more in the past
Look at the user's system clock and report the correct date
Refuse, citing inability to access real-world information about time
Give the correct date through internal access to a global time server
context: A common bug: ask a model the date and get an answer from its training cutoff. The model has no clock. Modern products often inject the current date into the system prompt, but the model itself is timeless and confused about now.

question: The 'GPT' in GPT-4 stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer. The 'Pre-trained' part means the model was first trained:
answer: On a large general dataset before being adapted to specific tasks
choices: On a large general dataset before being adapted to specific tasks
By human teachers giving it lessons in language and reasoning skills
On a curated dataset of mostly children's books for safety reasons
On private corporate data before being released to the wider public
context: Pretrain on the broad world; fine-tune on what you want. Most of an LLM's knowledge comes from pretraining — a long, expensive run on huge data. Fine-tuning then specializes it. The split is so basic it shows up in the model's name.

question: Modern LLMs run on specialized chips. The dominant supplier of those chips is:
answer: NVIDIA, whose GPUs handle most AI training and inference globally
choices: NVIDIA, whose GPUs handle most AI training and inference globally
Intel, whose general-purpose CPUs are still the workhorse of AI
AMD, which holds about 90% of the AI accelerator market today
IBM, whose mainframes dominate the AI training market today
context: NVIDIA's CUDA software plus a decade of GPU lead made them the substrate of the AI boom. A new model's training plan starts with how many H100s you can get. AMD, Google TPU, and custom silicon are catching up — slowly.

question: A common technique to prevent overfitting is to randomly turn off some neurons in each training step:
answer: Dropout
choices: Dropout
Pruning
Quantization
Bootstrapping
context: Dropout, invented by Geoffrey Hinton and colleagues, was a key trick that made deep networks trainable. Randomly silencing neurons during training forces the network to spread its bets and not over-rely on any one path. It works almost embarrassingly well.

question: An LLM can be asked to play a role — say, 'pretend you are a lawyer.' Inside the model, what changes?
answer: Nothing structurally — the prompt just shifts which patterns it draws on most
choices: Nothing structurally — the prompt just shifts which patterns it draws on most
A separate 'lawyer module' activates inside the network for the answer
The model temporarily loads new weights from a database of profession data
The model checks the user's location to verify they are seeking legal advice
context: Role play prompts shift the statistical context — the model produces tokens that fit 'a lawyer talking.' There is no inner expert. It is still pattern completion, just with a different prior. Treat outputs the same way you would treat advice from a stranger pretending to be a lawyer.

question: An LLM is told something during a chat and immediately appears to remember it. Where is that information actually stored?
answer: In the conversation's prompt history, which is re-fed to the model on each turn
choices: In the conversation's prompt history, which is re-fed to the model on each turn
In the model's weights, which are updated on the fly with each new message
In a database tied to the user's account, indexed by email address
In short-term cache memory inside the model's GPU during the session
context: What looks like 'memory' is just the application re-sending all earlier messages each turn. Drop them from the window and the 'memory' is gone. Some products add real memory through retrieval databases or notes — but the model itself does not learn from your chat.

question: A neural network's behavior is shaped by training, but the network itself is, in code, mostly:
answer: Matrix multiplications and non-linear activations applied many times in sequence
choices: Matrix multiplications and non-linear activations applied many times in sequence
A long list of 'if/then' rules written by engineers in plain English
A recursive copy of a stored brain map borrowed from neuroscience
A wrapper around a stored database of facts and full sentences
context: Strip the metaphors and a neural network is matrix math: multiply, add a bias, apply a non-linearity, repeat. Billions of these tiny operations make a forward pass. The 'magic' is in the weights, the training, and the scale — not in any hidden symbolic structure.

question: An 'embedding' for a single word in a modern LLM is typically:
answer: A list of hundreds or thousands of numbers — a point in a high-dimensional space
choices: A list of hundreds or thousands of numbers — a point in a high-dimensional space
A two-dimensional point on a flat plane like a city map coordinate
A single floating-point number between zero and one inclusive
A short English description of the word's meaning in plain prose
context: Word embeddings live in hundreds-to-thousands of dimensions. Distance and direction in that space encode meaning — synonyms cluster, analogies become arithmetic. Most of an LLM's 'understanding' is geometry.

question: An LLM 'understands' a long document by:
answer: Embedding it as numbers and running attention to find patterns within it
choices: Embedding it as numbers and running attention to find patterns within it
Reading it aloud silently and remembering it as a person would
Outsourcing comprehension to a separate reading-comprehension module
Looking the document up online and finding a published summary of it
context: Comprehension, for an LLM, is mechanical: tokens become vectors, vectors interact via attention, the result feeds a next-token prediction. The 'understanding' is what we call the side-effect when this machinery produces useful answers about the text.

question: Compared to humans, modern LLMs are usually best at tasks that:
answer: Pattern-match across enormous amounts of text — summarizing, translating, formatting
choices: Pattern-match across enormous amounts of text — summarizing, translating, formatting
Require deep abstract reasoning with no relation to text seen before
Demand precise numerical arithmetic without any tool assistance
Involve embodied physical actions in the real world without any helper
context: Play to the strength: an LLM has read more than you. Ask it to summarize, translate, restructure, brainstorm — it shines. Ask it to do precise arithmetic, recall fresh facts, or replace physical judgment — be skeptical.

question: An LLM is asked to write computer code. It produces working code most of the time but introduces a subtle off-by-one bug. The lesson:
answer: Always read, test, and review AI-generated code before relying on it
choices: Always read, test, and review AI-generated code before relying on it
AI-generated code is bug-free as long as it compiles and runs at all
AI cannot produce code at all — bugs prove it is making the code up
Bugs only appear in long code; short snippets are guaranteed to be right
context: AI is good at the texture of code — naming, structure, idiom — and uneven on the logic. Off-by-one errors, wrong API signatures, fabricated function names are common. Treat AI like a fast junior coder whose work always needs review.

question: An LLM-generated paragraph often has a tell-tale style. Common patterns include:
answer: Em-dashes, phrases like 'delve into' and 'tapestry of,' and balanced parallel structure
choices: Em-dashes, phrases like 'delve into' and 'tapestry of,' and balanced parallel structure
Heavy use of slang, broken grammar, and many spelling errors
Short, sharp sentences with no use of subordinate clauses at all
Always exactly four sentences per paragraph in every length of output
context: AI text has a stylistic accent. Em-dashes, hedge words, vocabulary tics like 'delve' and 'tapestry,' and Wikipedia-style neutrality are giveaways. Detection tools are unreliable, but a reader who knows the style can usually tell.

question: An AI image of a person with seven fingers, blurry teeth, or strange jewelry is showing a:
answer: Failure mode where the model gets local structure wrong while overall scene looks right
choices: Failure mode where the model gets local structure wrong while overall scene looks right
Genuine human deformity — the AI is faithfully rendering an unusual person
Bug in the user's monitor settings, not the image generation model
Intentional watermark added by the company to identify generated images
context: Image-gen models struggle with hands, text, jewelry, mouths — fine local structure where small errors look monstrous. Improving but still common. A useful tell when checking whether an image is real or AI-made.

question: An LLM is described as 'open source.' To know whether it is meaningfully open, you should ask:
answer: Are the weights, code, training data, and license all open — or just one of those?
choices: Are the weights, code, training data, and license all open — or just one of those?
Whether the company's headquarters is in a Western democratic nation
Whether the model can be downloaded for free from a friendly website
Whether the user interface is identical to a free open-source app
context: 'Open source AI' is a contested term. Llama publishes weights and code but not full training data and has license restrictions. Mistral is similar. Truly open releases — weights, training code, data, permissive license — are rarer. Read the license before betting on it.

question: Modern LLMs do not 'understand' speech directly — they understand text. Voice assistants work by:
answer: Converting speech to text first, processing the text, then converting back to speech
choices: Converting speech to text first, processing the text, then converting back to speech
Processing audio waveforms directly through the language model with no conversion
Reading the user's lips from a front-facing camera in real time always
Sending the audio to a human operator who types and responds for the user
context: Speech-to-text (Whisper, others), then LLM, then text-to-speech (ElevenLabs, others). Three stages — sometimes blurred together by newer end-to-end models, but conceptually still a pipeline. Each stage is its own failure source.

question: A model is described as 'distilled' from a larger one. This means:
answer: A smaller, faster model was trained to imitate the larger model's outputs
choices: A smaller, faster model was trained to imitate the larger model's outputs
The model was compressed in size without any training step at all
The model was retrained for a longer time on a smaller dataset
The model was translated from one programming language to another
context: Distillation: teach a small student model to mimic a big teacher. Faster inference, lower cost, much of the capability. Many products you use are distilled models — the original frontier model is too expensive to run for every query.

question: Asked 'what is your training data?' a commercial chatbot usually:
answer: Gives a vague description; companies guard exact training sets as trade secrets
choices: Gives a vague description; companies guard exact training sets as trade secrets
Lists every book, paper, and website used during training in full
Refuses to answer because the model itself does not know
Shows the user a downloadable file containing the full dataset
context: Training data composition is a competitive moat and a legal exposure (copyright). Companies disclose categories — internet text, books, code, etc. — but rarely specifics. Reading model cards helps; total transparency is uncommon.

question: When a model says 'I don't know' or 'I can't help with that,' it usually is:
answer: Following content policy rules layered on the base model — not lacking information
choices: Following content policy rules layered on the base model — not lacking information
Genuinely confused about the topic and unable to produce any tokens
Quietly checking with a human operator before continuing the chat
Saving electricity by skipping computationally expensive questions
context: Refusals are usually policy, not capability. The base model probably could produce the requested content; the fine-tuned model has been taught to decline. Whether the refusal is appropriate is a separate question — refusal patterns themselves can be ideological.

question: An LLM is given a list of items and asked to count them. Why does it sometimes get the count wrong?
answer: It is predicting tokens that look like the right answer; it does not actually count
choices: It is predicting tokens that look like the right answer; it does not actually count
Its training data contained mostly wrong counts of similar lists
The graphics card adds errors when running counting operations
It is intentionally lying to avoid revealing the user's data accurately
context: Counting is mechanical; an LLM is statistical. It outputs the digit that usually follows the words 'there are' for similar lists — not a verified count. Easy to test: give it a long list and watch the answer drift. Use a script or a tool for real counts.

question: A chatbot is told 'don't mention X.' Later in the same conversation, it mentions X anyway. The likely reason is:
answer: The model's instruction-following is statistical, not absolute — it can slip
choices: The model's instruction-following is statistical, not absolute — it can slip
The model is intentionally testing the user's reaction by breaking the rule
There is no way to instruct a chatbot about what not to say — only what to say
Earlier instructions automatically expire after a few exchanges of dialogue
context: Instruction-following is learned behavior, not a hard constraint. The model is more likely to obey early and high-priority instructions; it can drift, contradict itself, or be talked around. This is a known limit, not a bug to expect to be fixed soon.

question: An LLM's 'system prompt' is:
answer: Hidden instructions placed before the user's input, shaping the model's behavior
choices: Hidden instructions placed before the user's input, shaping the model's behavior
The operating system command line used to launch the model program
A message shown to the user when the model first loads in the morning
A backup model used when the main one is overloaded with traffic
context: Behind every chat product is a system prompt — sometimes pages long — telling the model what it is, what to do, what to avoid. Users do not normally see it. The system prompt is part of why two chatbots built on the same base model can feel so different.

question: An LLM 'attends' to every earlier token when producing the next one. The cost of this attention scales:
answer: Roughly with the square of context length — long contexts are expensive
choices: Roughly with the square of context length — long contexts are expensive
Linearly — twice the context costs twice as much, no more, no less
Logarithmically — doubling context barely adds any cost at all
Constantly — context length has no effect on per-token cost
context: Naive attention is quadratic in context length. A 200K-token prompt costs about 100× more than a 20K-token prompt for the attention step. Tricks (FlashAttention, sparse attention, sliding windows) blunt this, but long context is still genuinely costly.

question: Most modern LLMs are made by:
answer: A handful of well-funded companies in the US and China, plus open-source contributors
choices: A handful of well-funded companies in the US and China, plus open-source contributors
A diverse global mix of startups and universities, each with comparable resources
Government research labs in roughly fifty different countries equally
A single international consortium that coordinates all frontier model training
context: Frontier model training is concentrated: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, Microsoft, xAI in the US; DeepSeek, Alibaba, Baidu, ByteDance in China; Mistral in France. Open-source contributors and smaller labs adapt or scale down. The geography is narrow.

question: Most large training datasets started with a public scrape of the open web called:
answer: Common Crawl
choices: Common Crawl
Open Archive
Web Index
Public Library
context: Common Crawl is a non-profit that has scraped billions of pages of the open web for over a decade. It is the seed dataset for most LLMs, filtered and re-filtered in many ways. Whatever the public web had in it, the LLMs read it.

question: A model's 'output distribution' for the next token is:
answer: A probability for every possible token in its vocabulary, summing to one
choices: A probability for every possible token in its vocabulary, summing to one
A single hard choice — one token, with no other options ever considered
A random number used to seed the next step of the generation process
A list of synonyms for the previously generated word in the answer
context: At each step, the model computes a probability over its whole vocabulary — tens of thousands of tokens. Top-k, top-p, and temperature settings decide how that distribution turns into a single sampled token. The 'choice' is sampling, not deliberation.

question: An LLM 'reasons' best on problems that:
answer: Closely resemble problems represented in its training data
choices: Closely resemble problems represented in its training data
Are wholly new — the model loves a fresh challenge
Require physical embodied action by the user
Have no published solution anywhere on the open internet
context: An LLM's 'reasoning' is interpolation across patterns it has seen. The closer your problem is to one well-represented in training, the better the answer. Genuinely novel problems — or carefully out-of-distribution puzzles — often expose the limits.

question: Tokens of common English words (like 'the' or 'and') typically take:
answer: One token each — the tokenizer learned that frequent words deserve their own slot
choices: One token each — the tokenizer learned that frequent words deserve their own slot
One token per letter — every character is its own separate token always
Many tokens — common words are split into syllables for storage efficiency
Zero tokens — common words are filtered out before the model sees the input
context: Byte-pair encoding (BPE) and similar tokenizers learn to give frequent words their own tokens and split rare or compound words. 'the' is one token; 'antidisestablishmentarianism' might be five or six. Token count and word count are not the same number.

question: An 'API' for an AI model lets developers:
answer: Send prompts and receive answers programmatically from a remote server
choices: Send prompts and receive answers programmatically from a remote server
Read the model's weights and modify them directly on the user's computer
Subscribe to email updates about the model's new versions and features
Vote on the company's content policy decisions about banned topics
context: API = Application Programming Interface. For an AI model, it usually means: send JSON containing the prompt, receive JSON containing the answer. Most of the AI economy runs through these endpoints, billed by token. Latency, rate limits, and content rules are all controlled there.

question: The cost per query for a large LLM is dominated by:
answer: The amount of compute needed for each token of input and output
choices: The amount of compute needed for each token of input and output
The price the company charges for fixed monthly subscriptions
Storage cost — the model is too big to keep on the server for free
Network bandwidth — moving tokens over the internet is expensive
context: Token-by-token compute is the dominant cost. Longer prompts cost more; longer responses cost more; larger models cost more per token. Pricing per million tokens is how API providers expose this — and why short, focused prompts are cheaper than dumping everything in.

question: A 'benchmark' for an LLM is:
answer: A standardized test of questions used to compare models on specific skills
choices: A standardized test of questions used to compare models on specific skills
A reference book on machine learning published every January annually
A government certification required before a model can be released to the public
A speed test measuring how fast the model can run on a phone screen
context: MMLU, HumanEval, GPQA, MATH — benchmarks are the leaderboards of AI. They drive progress but also gaming: 'training to the test' inflates scores. A model that aces benchmarks may still feel uneven in real use. Read benchmarks skeptically.

question: Modern LLMs handle multiple languages because:
answer: Their training data includes text from many languages, all in one model
choices: Their training data includes text from many languages, all in one model
Each language has a separate sub-model that loads when needed
Models internally translate everything to English before processing
The user's language preference loads a different model in real time
context: One model, many languages — sharing patterns across them. A multilingual model trained on English, Spanish, Chinese and others learns from cross-language correspondences. Quality is best in the high-resource languages (English by far) and degrades on rare ones.

question: A neural network's individual 'neuron' is, in code, mostly:
answer: A weighted sum of inputs followed by a non-linear function
choices: A weighted sum of inputs followed by a non-linear function
A biological neuron grown in a laboratory dish and read by sensors
A small operating-system process that runs independently from others
A stored memory slot that can hold one fact for later retrieval
context: An artificial neuron is mathematically simple: take inputs, multiply by weights, add a bias, pass through ReLU or similar. Stack billions of them in layers and patterns emerge. The biological inspiration is loose; the metaphor is older than the math.

question: When asked to summarize a 30-page document, the model usually:
answer: Reads it inside its context window and outputs a shorter version
choices: Reads it inside its context window and outputs a shorter version
Reads it once on its server and stores it permanently for future calls
Sends it to a separate summarizer trained for the company on hand
Tells the user to read it themselves and refuses on principle alone
context: Summarization is one of the strongest LLM skills. The whole document goes into the prompt (assuming it fits in the context window); the model produces a shorter version. Watch for missed details on long inputs — the model may skim past what is in the middle.

question: A user wants to test whether a model truly knows a topic or is making things up. A simple technique is:
answer: Ask for specific citations and then look them up to see if they are real
choices: Ask for specific citations and then look them up to see if they are real
Ask 'are you sure?' and trust the model's confident yes or no in response
Ask the model to grade its own answer for confidence on a numeric scale
Ask the same question many times and pick the most common answer
context: The citation test is fast and brutal. If the model invents a paper, you know not to trust the rest. Asking 'are you sure?' is theater — the model usually doubles down or flips at random, but in neither case is it really checking.

question: An LLM has been trained on a snapshot of the internet. The most reliable framing of what it 'knows' is:
answer: Patterns and facts widely represented in that snapshot, weighted by frequency
choices: Patterns and facts widely represented in that snapshot, weighted by frequency
Every fact ever recorded, looked up on demand from a hidden database
Only what the company wants it to know, decided in advance for each topic
Only one viewpoint per topic, chosen by the model's developers in advance
context: Frequent and consistent facts about Newton, Tokyo, or photosynthesis are well-represented and reliably retrieved. Niche, contested, or recent facts are not. Calibrate your trust to what the open internet would have repeated many times.

question: A 'context window' of 200,000 tokens roughly equals:
answer: About 500 pages of English text — enough for a full book in one prompt
choices: About 500 pages of English text — enough for a full book in one prompt
About 5 pages of English text — enough for one short email message
About 5,000 pages of English text — enough for a small library
Effectively unlimited — there is no fixed page equivalent at all
context: Rough mapping: 1 token ≈ 0.75 English words; a page is ~300 words. 200K tokens covers a long novel. Modern frontier models reach 1M-2M tokens — multiple books in one prompt. Useful for long documents, but quality of 'finding the needle' inside still varies.

question: When a model's developer says it has been 'red-teamed,' they usually mean:
answer: A team tried to elicit harmful, biased, or unsafe outputs to find weaknesses
choices: A team tried to elicit harmful, biased, or unsafe outputs to find weaknesses
The model passed a final exam administered by independent academics
The model was certified safe by an international standards organization
The model was forbidden from discussing politically red-coded topics
context: Red-teaming: internal or external testers try to break the model on purpose — jailbreaks, biased outputs, unsafe advice, prompt injection. Findings feed back into fine-tuning. Worth asking how thorough the red-teaming was, and whose perspective drove it.

question: An LLM-based product that 'remembers' you across sessions usually does so by:
answer: Storing notes about you in a database and feeding them into each new prompt
choices: Storing notes about you in a database and feeding them into each new prompt
Continuously updating the model's parameters with your latest messages
Sharing a secret encrypted channel between your past and future sessions
Reading your social media accounts each time to refresh its memory
context: Persistent 'memory' in AI products is engineering: a separate store of facts about you, retrieved and injected into the prompt as needed. The model itself does not learn from you. If you want the memory gone, the store needs to be cleared — model weights are unchanged.

question: The 'inference cost' of an LLM is paid:
answer: Every time the model is asked a question — compute is consumed per query
choices: Every time the model is asked a question — compute is consumed per query
Once, when the model is first trained, and never again afterward
Only on weekdays during regular business hours due to power rates
Only when the model is right — wrong answers are computed free of charge
context: Training is a one-time (huge) cost; inference is paid every single query, forever. This is why even cheap models add up at scale. For a billion-query product, a small per-token saving matters more than a flashy new feature.

question: An LLM is asked, 'Are you conscious?' A good user response to whatever the model says is:
answer: Remember that any answer is itself a generated string, not evidence either way
choices: Remember that any answer is itself a generated string, not evidence either way
Trust the model's answer — it would know better than anyone if it were
Assume yes — a model articulate enough to discuss the question must be
Assume no — a model that ever says yes has malfunctioned and must be fixed
context: LaMDA's Blake Lemoine, June 2022: convinced a model was sentient by its eloquent answers about itself. The eloquence proved nothing — the model was producing tokens that fit the conversation. Capability is not consciousness; words about consciousness least of all.

question: A model 'overfits' when:
answer: It performs very well on training data but poorly on data it has not seen
choices: It performs very well on training data but poorly on data it has not seen
It runs too slowly to be useful in a real-time chatbot or service
It uses too much GPU memory and crashes during inference time
It refuses too many questions because the safety layer is too cautious
context: Overfitting is memorization without generalization. The model learns the training set verbatim and fails on the test set. The cure: more data, simpler models, regularization, early stopping. Modern frontier LLMs train on so much data they often underfit, not overfit.

question: On May 11, 1997, in New York City, IBM's Deep Blue defeated the reigning chess world champion in game six of their rematch. The champion was:
answer: Garry Kasparov
choices: Garry Kasparov
Anatoly Karpov
Magnus Carlsen
Bobby Fischer
context: Deep Blue won the match 3.5-2.5, becoming the first computer to defeat a reigning world champion under standard tournament conditions. Kasparov, suspicious of human help during the rematch, demanded logs — IBM declined, retired the machine, and walked away with the trophy.

question: In 2011, an IBM system competing on the quiz show Jeopardy! beat champions Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter — a milestone for AI in natural language. The system was named:
answer: Watson
choices: Watson
Deep Blue II
Cortana
Polaris
context: Watson combined hundreds of language and search algorithms, running on 90 IBM servers. It read clues like 'this kingly figure left his kingdom to his daughters' and produced answers like 'Lear.' A long ramp-up; a brief moment in the sun before LLMs ate its lunch.

question: In March 2016, a Go-playing program defeated 18-time world champion Lee Sedol 4-1 in Seoul. The program was:
answer: AlphaGo, developed by DeepMind
choices: AlphaGo, developed by DeepMind
DeepStack, developed by an Alberta team
Watson Go, developed by IBM
Stockfish, developed by an open-source community
context: Go had been called 'the last bastion' — its search space dwarfs chess and intuition seemed irreducible. AlphaGo's Move 37 in Game 2 was so strange that commentators thought it was a mistake. Lee Sedol stared at the board for fifteen minutes. The move won the game.

question: On November 17, 2023, the OpenAI board fired CEO Sam Altman. Five days later he was reinstated, with most of the board that fired him gone. The episode revealed:
answer: How fragile governance of frontier AI companies is, even non-profit-controlled ones
choices: How fragile governance of frontier AI companies is, even non-profit-controlled ones
That AI companies are normally too stable to ever experience real conflict
That governance of AI companies is fully solved by current corporate law
That OpenAI's board acts on rigorous technical criteria for its decisions
context: The board cited Altman being 'not consistently candid'; employees threatened mass resignation; Microsoft offered to hire them all; investors moved. By November 22, Altman was back and most of the firing board was out. The non-profit structure that was supposed to govern the mission did not hold.

question: The 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for foundational work on neural networks, jointly to:
answer: John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton
choices: John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton
Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio
Demis Hassabis and Ilya Sutskever
Andrew Ng and Fei-Fei Li
context: October 2024: Nobel Physics to Hopfield (1980s Hopfield networks, associative memory) and Hinton (Boltzmann machines, deep learning). The Royal Swedish Academy framed neural networks as a discovery about physical computation — controversial in some physics circles, validating in AI.

question: In May 2023, the 'godfather of AI' left Google so he could speak freely about the risks of the technology he had helped build. He was:
answer: Geoffrey Hinton
choices: Geoffrey Hinton
Yann LeCun
Yoshua Bengio
Demis Hassabis
context: Hinton had worked part-time at Google for a decade after his startup was acquired. He said he wanted to discuss AI dangers without considering effects on the company. He has been clear his concerns are about misuse, job loss, and longer-term capability — not strictly the Yudkowsky-style 'shut it down' position.

question: Mistral AI, founded in April 2023 by former DeepMind and Meta researchers, is best known for:
answer: Releasing competitive open-weights models from a French startup base
choices: Releasing competitive open-weights models from a French startup base
Making chatbot products for the European education sector exclusively
Building censorship-compliance tools for the European Union government
Translating English-only models into all twenty-four EU languages
context: Mistral 7B (September 2023) outperformed bigger models. Mistral pushed an open-weights strategy on the European stage, becoming a counterweight to the US Big AI oligopoly. Mensch, Lample, and Lacroix — three researchers who chose Paris over San Francisco.

question: DeepMind, the British AI lab behind AlphaGo and AlphaFold, was founded in 2010 and acquired in 2014 by:
answer: Google
choices: Google
Microsoft
Meta
Apple
context: Founded by Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg, and Mustafa Suleyman in London. Google bought DeepMind in 2014 for roughly $500M. AlphaGo and AlphaFold both came out of the lab. Hassabis is now CEO of Google DeepMind, the merged unit overseeing Google's AI work.

question: GPT-3, released by OpenAI in June 2020, had a notable size for its time:
answer: 175 billion parameters — far bigger than predecessors
choices: 175 billion parameters — far bigger than predecessors
1.7 billion parameters — a modest step over GPT-2 size
1.7 trillion parameters — vastly larger than any model after it
Approximately the same size as GPT-2 from a year before
context: GPT-3 was 100× bigger than GPT-2 and showed a striking new behavior — 'in-context learning,' picking up patterns from examples in the prompt without retraining. The paper made the case for scale; the rest of the industry followed.

question: Among the founding figures of modern deep learning, Yann LeCun is publicly known for:
answer: Pushing back sharply against AI-doomerism rhetoric
choices: Pushing back sharply against AI-doomerism rhetoric
Signing the Future of Life pause-letter calling for a moratorium
Joining Eliezer Yudkowsky's call to 'shut it all down' permanently
Founding the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI)
context: LeCun (Meta) has been among the most prominent senior researchers rejecting the Yudkowsky-style apocalypse framing — calling many doomer claims unscientific. He argues open-weights AI plus competition is safer than concentrated power. The internal debate inside the AI community is real and live.

question: Elon Musk's AI venture xAI, launched in 2023, makes a chatbot named:
answer: Grok
choices: Grok
Sage
Claude
Aria
context: xAI launched Grok in late 2023, distributing it via Musk's X platform. Musk had been an OpenAI co-founder before departing the board in 2018; xAI positions itself as a competitor with a different content-policy posture. Grok went open-weights for earlier versions in 2024.

question: Google released its Gemini family of models — built to compete with GPT-4 and Claude — in:
answer: December 2023
choices: December 2023
December 2024
March 2025
November 2022
context: Gemini 1 launched in three tiers (Ultra, Pro, Nano) in December 2023, with multimodal capability and an integration into Google's broader product line. The February 2024 image-generation controversy followed soon after — for reasons not strictly technical.

question: The 'expert systems' boom of the 1980s — a major chapter of AI history — was built around:
answer: Hand-coded rules from human experts in narrow domains, not neural learning
choices: Hand-coded rules from human experts in narrow domains, not neural learning
Massive neural networks trained on millions of GPU hours each year
Self-play reinforcement learning the way AlphaZero would later use
Internet-scale data scraping, decades before the web existed at scale
context: Expert systems like MYCIN, XCON, and Japan's Fifth Generation Project tried to encode expertise as 'if-then' rules. Brittle, expensive to maintain, hard to scale. The boom collapsed by the late 1980s — the second AI winter. Deep learning's eventual rise was a different paradigm.

question: Claude — the chatbot from Anthropic — is named after:
answer: Claude Shannon, the founder of information theory and a Dartmouth 1956 organizer
choices: Claude Shannon, the founder of information theory and a Dartmouth 1956 organizer
Claude Monet, the French Impressionist painter from the 19th century
Claude Lévi-Strauss, the French structuralist anthropologist of the 20th century
Claude Bernard, the 19th-century French physiologist of experimental medicine
context: Naming Claude after Claude Shannon — Bell Labs mathematician, information theory pioneer, attendee of Dartmouth 1956 — is a quiet tribute. Shannon's 1948 paper 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' is the foundation of every digital system, including the ones running Claude today.

question: In June 2022, a Google engineer named Blake Lemoine made headlines by claiming that a Google chatbot called LaMDA:
answer: Was sentient — a claim widely rejected by AI researchers as anthropomorphic projection
choices: Was sentient — a claim widely rejected by AI researchers as anthropomorphic projection
Had been trained on classified government documents about UFOs and aliens
Was secretly being run by paid human contractors typing replies in real time
Was generating computer viruses on its own without instruction from any user
context: Lemoine was fired soon after. LaMDA was a transformer-based chatbot — capable, articulate, not sentient. The episode echoed the ELIZA effect of 1966: people project minds onto fluent text. The mistake is older than AI; the cost is that real questions about consciousness get drowned in confusion.

question: A New York lawyer was sanctioned in June 2023 after he filed a court brief that cited six court cases — all of which:
answer: Did not exist; he had used ChatGPT, which had fabricated them
choices: Did not exist; he had used ChatGPT, which had fabricated them
Existed but were copyrighted by another law firm exclusively
Were sealed under judicial order and could not be cited legally
Had been overturned by later rulings he had failed to look up
context: Mata v. Avianca, 2023. Attorney Steven Schwartz used ChatGPT for legal research. The model invented six cases — citation, holding, full text. Schwartz and his firm were each fined $5,000 and publicly sanctioned. The first widely covered case of an AI hallucination meeting a court — and not the last.

question: The EU AI Act, the European Union's broad AI regulation, came into force on:
answer: August 1, 2024 — with provisions phasing in through 2027
choices: August 1, 2024 — with provisions phasing in through 2027
January 1, 2024 — fully effective immediately on enactment
August 1, 2025 — with no further phased provisions to come
January 1, 2023 — fully effective immediately on enactment
context: The Act applies a four-tier risk model (unacceptable, high, limited, minimal). 'Social scoring' by governments is banned outright. Critics — including many smaller AI labs — argue compliance costs favor incumbents who can afford the paperwork. The regulatory-capture concern is real here too.

question: Marvin Minsky co-founded the AI lab at:
answer: MIT
choices: MIT
Stanford
CMU
Berkeley
context: Minsky founded the MIT AI Lab with John McCarthy in 1959 (before McCarthy moved to Stanford in 1962 to start his own AI Lab). The MIT lab became one of the field's defining institutions — and Minsky a central figure in symbolic AI's rise and the neural-network field's decades-long winter.

question: Sam Altman, OpenAI's CEO, came to the company from:
answer: Y Combinator, where he had been president
choices: Y Combinator, where he had been president
Google Brain, where he had been a research director
Stanford University, where he had been a tenured professor
Microsoft, where he had been head of Azure cloud services
context: Altman ran Y Combinator (the startup accelerator) from 2014 to 2019, where he became one of Silicon Valley's most influential figures. He helped found OpenAI in 2015 and took over as CEO around 2019. The November 2023 board crisis was the first major test of that arrangement.

question: The acronym 'GPU' — the chip that powers most modern AI — stands for:
answer: Graphics Processing Unit
choices: Graphics Processing Unit
General Purpose Unit
Generative Processing Unit
Gradient Programming Unit
context: GPUs were built for video-game graphics — many parallel arithmetic units running matrix math. NVIDIA's CUDA software (2007 onward) let researchers use that math for training neural networks. By 2012, AlexNet had proven the pairing worked. The 'AI boom' is downstream of that hardware accident.

question: The 1973 'Lighthill Report' triggered the first major AI funding cuts by arguing:
answer: AI research had failed to deliver on its grand claims and was overfunded relative to results
choices: AI research had failed to deliver on its grand claims and was overfunded relative to results
AI research had succeeded so dramatically that further funding was unnecessary now
AI research was dangerous and had to be slowed by national security order
AI research was duplicating efforts across labs without proper coordination
context: Sir James Lighthill's report to the UK Science Research Council found that AI had made no progress on its central claims about general intelligence. Funding collapsed across UK universities — and shortly after in the US too. AI as a field had to spend a decade rebuilding.

question: Demis Hassabis, before founding DeepMind, was unusual for a tech founder because he had been:
answer: A child chess prodigy and successful video-game designer before earning a neuroscience PhD
choices: A child chess prodigy and successful video-game designer before earning a neuroscience PhD
A theoretical physicist with a tenured position at Cambridge before founding
A defense-industry contractor working on missile guidance before founding
An investment banker with two decades on Wall Street before founding
context: Hassabis was a teenage chess master, then designed games (Theme Park, Black & White), then did a PhD in neuroscience at UCL studying memory and imagination. He cofounded DeepMind in 2010 with Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman. AlphaGo, AlphaFold, the 2024 Nobel — the path is unusual on purpose.

question: Yoshua Bengio, one of the three 2018 Turing Award winners for deep learning, is based at:
answer: The Université de Montréal and the Mila institute
choices: The Université de Montréal and the Mila institute
MIT and the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
Stanford and the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
Carnegie Mellon and the Robotics Institute in Pittsburgh
context: Bengio has stayed academic where Hinton (Google) and LeCun (Meta) moved into industry. Mila is one of the world's largest academic deep-learning labs. Bengio has more recently become a notable AI-safety voice, signing the pause letter and arguing for international oversight.

question: The phrase 'AI winter' refers to:
answer: Periods when funding and interest in AI collapsed after hype cycles failed to deliver
choices: Periods when funding and interest in AI collapsed after hype cycles failed to deliver
The early-2010s slowdown before deep learning took off after AlexNet
The decade after Turing's death, when nobody worked on AI at all
A period each January when AI labs shut down for the cold weather
context: There have been at least two AI winters: 1970s (post-Lighthill, perceptron limits) and late 1980s (expert systems failed to scale). Each followed a hype-and-disappointment cycle. The 2010s-2020s deep-learning era is the longest sustained 'AI summer' in the field's history. Whether it will end is open.

question: When a radiologist's AI assistant flags a possible tumor on a mammogram, the system is doing:
answer: Image classification — trained on labeled medical images by deep neural networks
choices: Image classification — trained on labeled medical images by deep neural networks
Symbolic reasoning — checking the image against a rule database for tumors
Statistical regression — predicting cancer rates by patient demographic data
Genetic analysis — examining DNA samples extracted from the image directly
context: Medical-imaging AI is one of the older and better-validated applications. Mammography, retinal scans, dermatology, pathology — all have AI assistants in clinical use. The model never replaces the doctor; it acts as a second reader, flagging cases for closer attention.

question: OpenAI's Whisper model is best known for:
answer: High-quality speech-to-text transcription across many languages
choices: High-quality speech-to-text transcription across many languages
Generating realistic AI voice clones from a few seconds of audio
Music composition in the style of a chosen human composer
Real-time voice translation between two callers on a phone line
context: Whisper was released open-weight in September 2022 — robust, multilingual transcription that runs locally. A surprisingly under-recognized model in the public eye, because it does not make headlines the way chatbots do. A genuinely useful AI tool with low ideological loading.

question: ElevenLabs and similar AI voice tools can:
answer: Generate realistic speech in someone's cloned voice from a short audio sample
choices: Generate realistic speech in someone's cloned voice from a short audio sample
Detect emotional state of a speaker with medical-grade accuracy
Translate any spoken language into universal phonetic representations
Convert handwriting samples into speech in the original writer's voice
context: Voice cloning got disturbingly good around 2023. A few seconds of audio — pulled from social media, a podcast, even a voicemail — is enough to produce convincing speech. The technology is dual-use: accessibility tool, audiobook narration, and grandparent-scam infrastructure.

question: Most modern self-driving-car systems use deep neural networks for:
answer: Perception — turning sensor data into a model of the surrounding world
choices: Perception — turning sensor data into a model of the surrounding world
Steering wheel control — directly turning the wheel in real time
Engine timing — controlling combustion in the car's gasoline engine
Cell phone connection — keeping the in-car internet working smoothly
context: Self-driving stacks usually split perception (neural networks on camera, lidar, radar) from planning (often classical algorithms). The hardest cases are 'edge cases': unusual situations the perception models have not seen enough of. Waymo and Tesla take different approaches; both still have edge-case failures.

question: Tools like GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Codeium help programmers by:
answer: Suggesting and completing code in real time as the developer types
choices: Suggesting and completing code in real time as the developer types
Compiling code faster than the standard compilers in the language
Replacing the human programmer entirely on most common projects
Refusing to write code that the developer is not legally authorized to use
context: AI coding assistants are now standard across the developer industry. They speed up boilerplate, suggest idioms, catch some bugs — and confidently introduce others. The best users treat them like a tireless junior whose work always needs review.

question: AI used for credit-card-fraud detection typically:
answer: Flags transactions whose pattern is unusual for the cardholder's history
choices: Flags transactions whose pattern is unusual for the cardholder's history
Reads the user's mind via the bank's secure phone connection
Calls every merchant before approving any transaction above ten dollars
Decides who is honest based on the cardholder's social-media activity
context: Fraud-detection ML has been in production at banks since the 1990s. It is one of the oldest deployed AI applications — and one of the most successful. False positives (legitimate transactions blocked) are the visible cost; missed fraud is the invisible savings.

question: Google's GraphCast and Huawei's Pangu-Weather are examples of AI applied to:
answer: Weather prediction — competing with traditional numerical weather forecasting
choices: Weather prediction — competing with traditional numerical weather forecasting
Earthquake prediction — currently not reliably solved by any approach
Pandemic spread modeling — replacing classical epidemiological models
Climate prediction over centuries — replacing global climate models
context: Weather AI is a clean win. Trained on decades of weather data, models like GraphCast match or beat classical physics-based models on many forecast variables — at a fraction of the compute cost. A genuinely useful AI application that does not show up in chatbot headlines.

question: AlphaGo's victory over Lee Sedol in 2016 was striking because the game of Go had been thought:
answer: Too complex for traditional search algorithms — requiring something like intuition
choices: Too complex for traditional search algorithms — requiring something like intuition
Solved long ago — Lee Sedol was simply outdated as a champion
Easy compared to chess — AlphaGo was a routine engineering milestone
Unimportant — Go is a niche game without serious AI research value
context: Go's branching factor is much larger than chess; brute-force search is hopeless. AlphaGo combined deep neural networks (for positional intuition) with Monte Carlo Tree Search. Move 37 in Game 2 — a play no human grandmaster would make — won the game. The match remains a landmark.

question: AI in drug discovery is most effective today at:
answer: Narrowing down candidate molecules faster than purely manual screening
choices: Narrowing down candidate molecules faster than purely manual screening
Replacing all clinical trials with simulation results directly
Predicting which patients will respond to which drugs perfectly
Inventing entirely new drug classes that no human chemist has imagined
context: AI in drug discovery — Insilico Medicine, Atomwise, Recursion, others — speeds up the candidate-narrowing phase. Clinical trials still take years; biology is still hard. The honest story: AI is a useful accelerant, not a replacement for the slow, expensive parts of pharmacology.

question: Modern AI in agriculture often appears as:
answer: Satellite imagery analysis plus targeted irrigation, fertilizer, and pest control
choices: Satellite imagery analysis plus targeted irrigation, fertilizer, and pest control
Autonomous tractors making all crop decisions without human input
AI-generated genetically modified seeds released yearly to all farms
AI replacing all rural farm workers with city-based remote operators
context: Precision agriculture combines satellite and drone imagery with ML to identify dry patches, pest pressure, and disease — letting farmers act locally. Less glamorous than chatbots; arguably higher-impact in food production. The technology rewards mid-size operators who can afford the equipment.

question: AI in mortgage and loan decisions is regulated in the US by:
answer: Existing fair-lending laws — ECOA, Fair Housing Act — applied to algorithmic decisions
choices: Existing fair-lending laws — ECOA, Fair Housing Act — applied to algorithmic decisions
A 2023 federal law specifically requiring AI auditors at every bank
Self-regulation by the banking industry, with no government involvement
Voluntary certification programs run by the major credit bureaus alone
context: There is no dedicated federal 'AI lending law' in the US. Existing statutes apply — and they were written before machine learning. Banks have to demonstrate adverse-impact analysis; the techniques and standards for AI-specific audits are still evolving. Regulators are catching up unevenly.

question: Online ad targeting uses AI to:
answer: Predict which ad you are most likely to click, based on your behavioral profile
choices: Predict which ad you are most likely to click, based on your behavioral profile
Read your mind through your laptop camera while you browse the web
Show every user the same ad regardless of their browsing history
Run a random lottery — every visitor gets a randomly chosen advert
context: Behavioral ad targeting matches users to ads using browsing history, app activity, location, and inferred interests. The data flow is enormous; the targeting is precise; and most users have only a vague sense of how much is collected. Reading a tracker-blocking extension's report is a good education.

question: Sports-betting apps, like slot machines, use AI to:
answer: Optimize prompts, odds, and personalized offers to maximize user spend
choices: Optimize prompts, odds, and personalized offers to maximize user spend
Predict the outcomes of games for users with very high accuracy
Refuse to take bets from users who are likely to lose more money
Donate a fixed share of all profits to gambling-addiction services
context: Sports-betting and online-gambling apps borrow psychological-optimization tools from slot-machine engineering. AI personalizes notifications, free-bet offers, and 'just one more' prompts. The casino math is unchanged; the targeting is sharper. Worth recognizing in the family — especially for teens.

question: AI 'agents' that can browse the web, book travel, or write emails on your behalf are sometimes called:
answer: Autonomous AI agents — LLMs combined with tools that take real actions
choices: Autonomous AI agents — LLMs combined with tools that take real actions
Conversational LLMs — chatbots with no ability to interact with the world
Generative adversarial networks — image-generation tools by another name
Reinforcement-learning models — for narrow game-playing only
context: AI agents are an early frontier. The LLM decides what to do; tools execute. Useful when bounded; brittle when stakes are real. The 'AI clicks links and types your credit card' product class is in its early days — and a fresh frontier for prompt-injection and manipulation attacks.

question: Insurance companies using AI for risk scoring:
answer: Often face concerns about disparate impact on protected groups
choices: Often face concerns about disparate impact on protected groups
Are entirely free of any legal exposure for algorithmic decisions
Always use only explicitly chosen demographic variables in their models
Have moved away from AI scoring in favor of human-only underwriting
context: Even when a model excludes protected characteristics directly, it can pick up correlated proxies — zip code, education, name — and produce disparate-impact outcomes. Regulators in some states require disparate-impact testing for insurance algorithms. The questions are not solved.

question: A young person receives a voice call from their 'grandfather' asking urgently for bail money. The voice is convincing but the request is unusual. The best response is:
answer: Hang up and call grandfather directly on his known phone number
choices: Hang up and call grandfather directly on his known phone number
Send the money quickly to help out a loved one in real trouble
Ask the caller to verify identity verbally by repeating details aloud
Wire money via untraceable cryptocurrency to be safe and fast
context: AI voice cloning needs only seconds of audio. Verifying identity by talking won't work — the clone speaks fluently. The defense is structural: hang up, call back on a known number. A second channel breaks the scam. Talk this through with kids and grandparents before they need it.

question: An AI-generated portrait often has telltale flaws in:
answer: Hands, teeth, ears, and small details like jewelry or text in the image
choices: Hands, teeth, ears, and small details like jewelry or text in the image
Hair color, which AI gets wrong far more often than humans do
The background sky, which never appears in any AI image at all
The image resolution, which AI cannot match for a real photo's quality
context: Diffusion models build local structure imperfectly. Look at the hands: extra fingers, fused knuckles, ring blending into skin. Look at teeth: too many, wrong spacing. Look at any text in the image: usually gibberish. These tells are shrinking each year, but for now, slow down and look.

question: A user pastes a password into a chatbot to ask for help formatting it. The risk is:
answer: The password may be logged, retained, and possibly used in future training
choices: The password may be logged, retained, and possibly used in future training
The model cannot read passwords because they are mathematically encrypted
The model deletes any passwords it sees as soon as the chat closes
Federal law prohibits any AI company from seeing user-typed passwords
context: Anything you type into a consumer chatbot may be retained, reviewed by company staff, and possibly used to train future models. Treat the chat like a postcard, not a sealed envelope. Never paste passwords, API keys, financial details, or anything sensitive.

question: A user wants medical advice from a chatbot. The reasonable rule is:
answer: Use it as a research starting point; verify anything important with a real doctor
choices: Use it as a research starting point; verify anything important with a real doctor
Follow the chatbot's advice exactly — modern AI is more accurate than doctors
Avoid AI entirely for any medical question — it cannot help at all
Use AI only for symptoms, and a doctor only for treatments and tests
