context: Japan's Fifth Generation Computer Project (1982-1992) also fell short. Rule-based knowledge engineering hit a brick wall on real-world messiness.

question: Terry Winograd's SHRDLU, a 1970 MIT thesis project, conversed in English about a simulated 'blocks world' of toy geometric objects on a virtual table. The program could pick up the red block, put it on the green block, and answer questions about its own actions. What was SHRDLU's central limitation?
answer: It only worked inside its constrained blocks world; trying to extend it to the open world broke nearly every component of the system.
choices: It only worked inside its constrained blocks world; trying to extend it to the open world broke nearly every component of the system.
It only worked in Japanese, which limited its commercial appeal in the English-speaking academic world.
It only worked on weekends, which is when MIT's mainframe was reserved for AI research projects.
It only worked with rectangular blocks, which is why later researchers shifted to other geometric shapes.
context: SHRDLU showcased the limits of toy-world success. Winograd later turned away from AI and toward human-computer interaction.

question: On May 11, 1997, IBM's Deep Blue defeated reigning world chess champion Garry Kasparov in the sixth and final game of their rematch, winning the match 3.5-2.5. Kasparov resigned the deciding game after only 19 moves. What was Deep Blue's core approach to the chess problem?
answer: Brute-force search of millions of board positions per second, evaluating each with a hand-tuned scoring function written by IBM's team.
choices: Brute-force search of millions of board positions per second, evaluating each with a hand-tuned scoring function written by IBM's team.
A neural network that had learned chess by playing millions of self-play games against weaker versions of itself.
A genetic algorithm that bred chess-playing programs, with the strongest mating and the weakest discarded.
A reinforcement learning agent that updated its strategy after every move using a reward signal from the score.
context: Deep Blue was 1990s symbolic AI at its peak. The 'search plus eval' template was older than the field; Deep Blue had the hardware to push it to victory.

question: In February 2011, IBM Watson appeared on Jeopardy! and defeated two of the show's greatest champions, Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter. Watson's win is remembered as a milestone in machine handling of natural language. What technical capability did Watson demonstrate that Deep Blue did not need?
answer: Reading and parsing the show's notoriously punning clues in plain English, then assembling plausible answers from a vast text corpus.
choices: Reading and parsing the show's notoriously punning clues in plain English, then assembling plausible answers from a vast text corpus.
Speaking aloud to the audience in a synthesized voice that sounded indistinguishable from a human contestant.
Beating chess masters during commercial breaks between rounds of the Jeopardy! show.
Recognizing the faces of the live audience and tailoring its answers to each viewer's individual preferences.
context: Watson combined retrieval, hypothesis generation, and confidence ranking, all in service of natural-language Q&A. It anticipated retrieval-augmented LLMs.

question: GPU-based parallel computing turned out to be essential to deep learning's 2010s rise. Andrew Ng, Adam Coates, and others showed in 2009 that GPUs trained neural networks an order of magnitude faster than CPUs. Why was this hardware shift such a tipping point for the field?
answer: Faster training let researchers try bigger networks on more data, exposing capabilities that smaller experiments could never have seen.
choices: Faster training let researchers try bigger networks on more data, exposing capabilities that smaller experiments could never have seen.
GPUs gave neural networks new mathematical capabilities that CPUs structurally could not provide, no matter the speed.
GPUs eliminated the need for any training data, by computing the correct weights directly from the network's architecture.
GPUs were cheaper than CPUs, so researchers could afford more of them than the previous generation could.
context: NVIDIA's CUDA platform (2007 onward) made GPU programming accessible. The hardware substrate of modern AI was built around CUDA.

question: OpenAI released GPT-2 in February 2019. The lab initially withheld the largest 1.5-billion-parameter model, citing concerns about misuse for generating fake news and spam. What was the public response to the staggered release?
answer: Many researchers criticized the move as overhyped safety theater; the full model was released later that year with minimal real-world incident.
choices: Many researchers criticized the move as overhyped safety theater; the full model was released later that year with minimal real-world incident.
Most researchers praised the move as cautious, and the full model was permanently classified and never released.
Researchers were unanimous in calling it dangerous, and OpenAI was sued by national security agencies for delaying release.
Researchers ignored the move entirely, and the full model received no public attention when it finally appeared.
context: GPT-2 was the first OpenAI model to frame safety as a release-staging concern. Critics called the framing performative; the framing also set a precedent.

question: GPT-4 launched in March 2023, four months after ChatGPT. OpenAI declined to publish the model's size, training data, or architecture in detail, calling its system card 'minimal' for competitive reasons. What was the most striking publicly demonstrable advance over GPT-3.5?
answer: Multimodality (the ability to read images as well as text) plus stronger performance on professional exams like the bar and the SAT.
choices: Multimodality (the ability to read images as well as text) plus stronger performance on professional exams like the bar and the SAT.
True long-term memory across sessions, which was demonstrated to persist for months without external storage.
Fully autonomous physical robot control through a built-in motor cortex that previous GPT models did not have.
Genuine consciousness, which OpenAI demonstrated in a peer-reviewed paper at NeurIPS 2023.
context: GPT-4 was a closed model. Its image capability was real and audited; its model size remained secret. Mixture-of-experts architecture was rumored.

question: DeepMind's AlphaZero, published in December 2017, learned chess, Go, and shogi from scratch with no human game data. After hours of self-play, it surpassed the strongest existing engines. What was the central difference between AlphaZero and earlier game-playing AI like Deep Blue?
answer: It learned from self-play with a neural network guiding tree search, instead of from human-written evaluation functions and opening books.
choices: It learned from self-play with a neural network guiding tree search, instead of from human-written evaluation functions and opening books.
It was given the entire history of all played games and memorized them, then replayed the best lines as needed.
It used a quantum computer to evaluate every possible position in parallel, regardless of the game's branching factor.
It was hand-coded by a team of grandmasters who wrote down every position the engine could ever reach.
context: AlphaZero's general framework (Monte Carlo tree search plus a learned policy and value network) generalized to multiple games with minimal modification.

question: Geoffrey Hinton, often called the 'godfather of deep learning,' spent decades championing neural networks through periods when most of the field had moved on. In 2018, he shared the Turing Award with Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio. What did Hinton do in May 2023 that made headlines well beyond the AI community?
answer: He resigned from Google, citing a desire to speak freely about risks from advancing AI capabilities; the New York Times broke the story.
choices: He resigned from Google, citing a desire to speak freely about risks from advancing AI capabilities; the New York Times broke the story.
He was awarded a second Turing Award, becoming the only person to receive the prize twice in computer science history.
He moved from Toronto to Beijing to lead a new state AI research lab funded by the Chinese government.
He published a paper proving that neural networks could not become superintelligent, ending the AI safety debate.
context: Hinton's 2023 departure framed AI risk in mainstream terms, though his stance differs from Yudkowsky's apocalypticism. He was awarded the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics with John Hopfield.

question: On November 17, 2023, OpenAI's board fired CEO Sam Altman in a brief public statement saying he had not been 'consistently candid' with them. Within five days he was back. What sequence of events brought him back so fast?
answer: Nearly all 800 employees threatened to follow him to Microsoft; the board reversed course and reinstated him on November 22.
choices: Nearly all 800 employees threatened to follow him to Microsoft; the board reversed course and reinstated him on November 22.
A government investigation cleared him of any wrongdoing, and the board legally had to reinstate him within five days.
Sam Altman bought out the board with his personal fortune and replaced the directors with his own appointees.
Microsoft acquired OpenAI in a midnight deal and installed Altman as its new CEO under the Microsoft umbrella.
context: The five-day saga exposed OpenAI's nonprofit governance as fragile. Sutskever, Adam D'Angelo, Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner were the board members behind the firing.

question: Eliezer Yudkowsky has spent two decades as the most prominent voice arguing that AI development will likely lead to human extinction. He founded the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI) in 2000. In March 2023 he published a Time magazine essay that captured his position in one phrase. What did he call for?
answer: An indefinite, internationally enforced shutdown of all large AI training runs, with strikes on noncompliant data centers if necessary.
choices: An indefinite, internationally enforced shutdown of all large AI training runs, with strikes on noncompliant data centers if necessary.
A six-month pause coordinated by the United Nations, with training to resume once safety standards were agreed on.
A return to symbolic AI methods that were dominant in the 1970s, abandoning neural networks entirely.
A nationalization of all AI labs under joint government control, with research continuing but profits eliminated.
context: Yudkowsky's Time essay (March 2023) called for bombing rogue data centers if needed. The bank treats both his doomerism and accelerationism as ideologies.

question: Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of the crypto exchange FTX, was a self-described effective altruist and one of the largest donors to AI safety causes through the FTX Future Fund. In November 2022, FTX collapsed in a matter of days. He was convicted of fraud in November 2023. What did the collapse expose about the EA-AI safety pipeline?
answer: EA leaders had been warned about Bankman-Fried's ethics years earlier; FTX-funded grant networks unraveled when the fraud became public.
choices: EA leaders had been warned about Bankman-Fried's ethics years earlier; FTX-funded grant networks unraveled when the fraud became public.
EA had no involvement with FTX, and the collapse had no impact on AI safety research funding or institutional networks.
FTX's funding had gone entirely to climate research, not AI safety, so AI safety was unaffected by the collapse.
FTX's collapse was a hoax invented by AI safety critics to discredit the field; SBF was actually innocent of all charges.
context: Future Fund had pledged $100M in 2022. EA leadership warnings about SBF dated to 2018. The bank flags the EA grift exposed.

question: William MacAskill, an Oxford philosopher and author of What We Owe the Future (2022), helped popularize longtermism within the effective altruism movement. He was on the board of the FTX Future Fund. What is longtermism, the doctrine he champions?
answer: The view that influencing the very long-run future, including potential trillions of future people, is among the most important moral priorities now.
choices: The view that influencing the very long-run future, including potential trillions of future people, is among the most important moral priorities now.
The view that humans should live as long as biologically possible, with anti-aging research as the central moral priority.
The view that current generations should make no sacrifices for future ones, since the future is too uncertain.
The view that environmental concerns are paramount and outweigh any other consideration in moral reasoning.
context: Longtermism's critics argue it can justify any present-day cost in the name of speculative future benefits. Bostrom's astronomical-waste argument is a foundational paper.

question: The Future of Life Institute, founded in 2014 by Max Tegmark, Jaan Tallinn, and others, has been a leading voice for AI safety advocacy. On March 22, 2023, FLI published an open letter calling for an industry pause on training large AI models. How long a pause did the letter request?
answer: At least six months on training any system more capable than GPT-4, to be globally agreed and publicly verifiable.
choices: At least six months on training any system more capable than GPT-4, to be globally agreed and publicly verifiable.
A permanent halt on all AI training worldwide, enforced by an international treaty modeled on nuclear nonproliferation.
A two-week pause for an emergency safety summit, after which training would resume with new disclosures.
A pause only on commercial deployment, with research and training continuing at full pace inside the labs.
context: FLI's letter reached 30,000 signatures including Musk, Wozniak, Bengio, Tegmark. Yudkowsky declined to sign, calling it too weak.

question: Cyc, an ambitious symbolic AI project started by Doug Lenat in 1984, attempted to encode common-sense knowledge as millions of hand-written logical assertions. The project ran for nearly four decades. By the 2020s, it had largely been overtaken by deep learning systems. What is the lesson the contrast carries for AI history?
answer: Hand-coding world knowledge proved too brittle and slow to scale; learned representations from massive data succeeded where Cyc did not.
choices: Hand-coding world knowledge proved too brittle and slow to scale; learned representations from massive data succeeded where Cyc did not.
Cyc was never tried in practice and so cannot be compared with deep learning systems that succeeded in deployment.
Cyc actually outperformed deep learning on every benchmark, but lacked the marketing to gain commercial traction.
Cyc was identical to GPT-3 in every architectural detail, so the projects' fates are equivalent in retrospect.
context: Lenat's Cyc cost hundreds of millions in encoded knowledge. The deep learning revolution was the experimental disproof of pure symbolic AI's scaling story.

question: AlphaGo's 2016 victory over Lee Sedol included a moment that the Go community still discusses. In Game 2, move 37 by AlphaGo was so unusual that commentators initially thought the program had crashed. Lee Sedol himself reportedly stepped away from the board. What was striking about the move?
answer: It violated centuries of human Go orthodoxy by playing on the fifth line, yet proved strategically sound on later analysis.
choices: It violated centuries of human Go orthodoxy by playing on the fifth line, yet proved strategically sound on later analysis.
It was a forced move that AlphaGo had been pre-programmed to play in that specific opening, with no learning involved.
It was a bug that gave away the game, and AlphaGo lost Game 2 because of it, despite winning the match overall.
It was a move AlphaGo had stolen from one of Lee Sedol's old games, returning his own strategy against him.
context: Move 37 became a symbol of a new aesthetic in Go. The Go community has since adopted some of AlphaGo's unusual moves into mainstream play.

question: Sergey Brin, co-founder of Google, returned to active work on AI in 2023 after years of semi-retirement. He reportedly contributed code to Google's Gemini project. What signal did his return send to the industry?
answer: That Google's leadership viewed the AI moment as critical enough to pull a founder back into hands-on engineering.
choices: That Google's leadership viewed the AI moment as critical enough to pull a founder back into hands-on engineering.
That Google had run out of engineers and needed to recruit retired employees to fill basic technical roles.
That Brin had decided to compete with Sam Altman personally, with no involvement from Google's leadership.
That Google was planning to fire all of its other AI engineers and replace them with the founders.
context: Brin's hands-on return paralleled Larry Page's reduced involvement. Senior leadership engagement signaled the moment to the broader industry.

question: Robert J. Williams, a Black man living in Farmington Hills, Michigan, was arrested on January 9, 2020, by Detroit police on the basis of a facial recognition match. He spent 30 hours in detention. What had actually happened?
answer: A facial recognition system matched a poor-quality store-camera still to his expired driver's license photo, despite no physical resemblance.
choices: A facial recognition system matched a poor-quality store-camera still to his expired driver's license photo, despite no physical resemblance.
Williams had been correctly identified by the system and police never released him from the wrongful arrest.
Williams had voluntarily turned himself in for crimes he did not commit, in a case of mistaken self-identification.
Williams was actually a fictional case invented by the ACLU to publicize facial recognition concerns.
context: Williams was the first publicly documented wrongful arrest from facial recognition in the US. Detroit later settled the lawsuit for $300K plus reforms.

question: Steven Schwartz, a New York attorney, submitted a legal brief in Mata v. Avianca in 2023 that cited several court decisions. The decisions did not exist. He had used ChatGPT for research and had not verified the citations. What was the consequence in court?
answer: Judge P. Kevin Castel sanctioned Schwartz, partner Peter LoDuca, and their firm Levidow & Oberman $5,000 each in June 2023.
choices: Judge P. Kevin Castel sanctioned Schwartz, partner Peter LoDuca, and their firm Levidow & Oberman $5,000 each in June 2023.
The court ruled in Schwartz's favor, finding that ChatGPT was a reliable legal source.
Schwartz was disbarred permanently from practicing law in any US jurisdiction.
The court ordered ChatGPT to be shut down nationwide pending an investigation.
context: Mata v. Avianca, June 22, 2023. The case became the textbook warning on AI hallucination in legal practice. Schwartz acknowledged his error publicly.

question: Lina Khan, chair of the Federal Trade Commission from 2021 to early 2025, became a notable voice on AI antitrust concerns. The FTC opened inquiries into the largest AI labs and their cloud-provider relationships. What core concern did Khan focus on?
answer: Whether major cloud providers' investments in OpenAI and Anthropic amounted to anticompetitive coordination in the AI market.
choices: Whether major cloud providers' investments in OpenAI and Anthropic amounted to anticompetitive coordination in the AI market.
Whether AI chatbots were illegal under existing consumer protection law and should all be shut down.
Whether the FTC itself should be replaced with an AI system that could regulate more effectively than humans.
Whether all AI investments should be nationalized under federal control by the end of her term.
context: FTC inquiries into Microsoft-OpenAI and Amazon-Anthropic relationships were a hallmark of Khan's tenure. Big AI concentration as antitrust matter is the new framing.

question: Geoffrey Hinton's May 2023 departure from Google was first reported by Cade Metz in the New York Times. Hinton wanted to speak freely about what he saw as growing risks from AI. What specific concern did Hinton highlight that distinguished him from Yudkowsky's framing?
answer: He emphasized near-term concerns like misinformation and autonomous weapons, while remaining cautious about apocalyptic timelines.
choices: He emphasized near-term concerns like misinformation and autonomous weapons, while remaining cautious about apocalyptic timelines.
He called for immediate global shutdown of all AI training within thirty days, going further than even Yudkowsky.
He claimed AI was already superintelligent in 2023 and was secretly running world governments.
He said all AI research should be redirected toward agricultural applications, with no remaining safety concerns.
context: Hinton's nuance is often lost in retellings. He has cited 30-to-50-year timelines compressed to faster ones, but distinguishes his stance from Yudkowsky's.

question: Sora, OpenAI's text-to-video model announced in February 2024, was not released to the public for nearly ten months. The phased release reflected what OpenAI called 'red-teaming' for safety. What practical concern most shaped the delay?
answer: Worries about misuse for non-consensual imagery, election misinformation, and deepfake harassment shaped the cautious rollout.
choices: Worries about misuse for non-consensual imagery, election misinformation, and deepfake harassment shaped the cautious rollout.
Sora was technically broken and could not produce video at all; the demonstrations were a deception.
OpenAI was waiting for the EU to ban Sora before releasing it to Americans only.
OpenAI ran out of GPUs to serve Sora to users, so the release was delayed for hardware reasons alone.
context: Video models raise more acute deepfake concerns than image models. Sora's December 2024 release came with watermarking and refusal heuristics.

question: The MLPerf benchmark consortium, founded in 2018, standardized how to compare AI hardware and software stacks on common tasks. By 2024 it had become one of the main public yardsticks for AI training and inference performance. What was its founding motivation?
answer: To stop the proliferation of self-serving benchmark numbers from each vendor and replace them with one common, auditable yardstick.
choices: To stop the proliferation of self-serving benchmark numbers from each vendor and replace them with one common, auditable yardstick.
To force all AI labs to share their training code, ending closed-source AI altogether.
To regulate AI training run sizes worldwide, with a hard cap on parameter counts.
To establish a single Asian company as the sole provider of AI benchmarking services.
context: MLPerf grew out of the perception that vendor claims were not comparable. Standardization is a perennial fight in compute benchmarking.

question: Character.AI, founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, built popular chatbot 'characters' that users could converse with. In 2024 the company changed shape. What did Google announce about Character.AI?
answer: Google paid roughly $2.7 billion to license Character.AI's technology and rehire Shazeer; Character.AI itself continued in reduced form.
choices: Google paid roughly $2.7 billion to license Character.AI's technology and rehire Shazeer; Character.AI itself continued in reduced form.
Google acquired Character.AI outright for fifty billion dollars in cash and an equity-swap deal that closed in the first quarter of 2024.
Google sued Character.AI for trademark infringement over the use of its own engineers' names, which ended the smaller company within months.
Google invested in Character.AI's initial public offering at a two-hundred-billion-dollar valuation, a record for any AI startup IPO in 2024.
context: Shazeer, a transformer-paper co-author, returned to Google. Character.AI joined Inflection and Adept in the soft-acquihire pattern.

question: AI-assisted radiology has been one of the earliest commercial deployments of deep learning in medicine. Models help flag potential tumors on mammograms, skin lesions, and retinal scans. What is the most honest framing of where AI fits in real radiology workflows today?
answer: As a second reader that flags possibilities for the radiologist to verify, not as a replacement for trained medical judgment.
choices: As a second reader that flags possibilities for the radiologist to verify, not as a replacement for trained medical judgment.
As the primary reader of all medical images, with radiologists eliminated entirely from large hospital systems by 2024.
As a hobbyist tool with no real role in any clinical setting, since AI has never been deployed in any hospital.
As a marketing gimmick used in advertising but never deployed clinically, since regulators have banned all such use.
context: FDA-cleared AI radiology tools exist for breast, lung, brain, and retinal imaging. The human-in-the-loop model remains standard.

question: OpenAI's Whisper, released in September 2022 as open source, was a major step in automatic speech recognition. The model handles dozens of languages and is robust to noise. What was unusual about how Whisper was trained that made it more robust than earlier ASR systems?
answer: It trained on 680,000 hours of weakly-labeled multilingual audio from the web rather than carefully curated studio recordings.
choices: It trained on 680,000 hours of weakly-labeled multilingual audio from the web rather than carefully curated studio recordings.
It trained on a single hour of audio recorded in a Stanford laboratory, which is what made it robust to real-world noise.
It trained on text alone, with no audio at all, and learned speech recognition purely through written language patterns.
It trained on a quantum computer using audio that had been encoded as superpositions, which is why it was so robust.
context: Whisper's diverse training corpus made it robust to accents, noise, and code-switching. The open release shaped a generation of speech tools.

question: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok are the most-used chatbot assistants by 2025. They share architecture but differ in training and personality. What is the most useful skill for a user comparing assistants on the same question?
answer: Treat each as one opinion, compare their answers, and look for places they agree and disagree before settling on a conclusion.
choices: Treat each as one opinion, compare their answers, and look for places they agree and disagree before settling on a conclusion.
Use only one chatbot for everything, since switching between them is unnecessary if you have found the best one.
Average the chatbots' numerical outputs, which works for any factual question regardless of subject.
Always go with whichever chatbot answers fastest, since speed correlates perfectly with accuracy.
context: Different post-training shapes different blind spots. Cross-checking is now standard practice for serious chatbot users.

question: Fraud detection has used machine learning for decades, well before the deep-learning era. Banks, credit card networks, and payment processors all rely on it. What is the central limitation that fraud-detection systems have always faced, and that modern AI does not eliminate?
answer: Adversaries adapt: fraudsters change tactics when detection improves, so the detection system is always chasing yesterday's fraud patterns.
choices: Adversaries adapt: fraudsters change tactics when detection improves, so the detection system is always chasing yesterday's fraud patterns.
Computing power, since fraud detection requires more compute than any existing data center can provide.
Mathematical proofs, since fraud detection can never work without formal mathematical guarantees that do not exist.
User consent, since fraud detection requires explicit opt-in from every customer at every transaction.
context: Adversarial pressure is the central challenge of any deployed fraud system. AI shifts the cat-and-mouse equilibrium but does not end it.

question: AI-generated text detection (GPTZero, OpenAI's own classifier briefly in 2023) has been an active research area as schools and publishers worry about AI essays. The detectors have struggled. Why has detection been such an uneven cat-and-mouse game?
answer: Text can be paraphrased lightly to defeat statistical signatures, and detectors produce many false positives on human writing.
choices: Text can be paraphrased lightly to defeat statistical signatures, and detectors produce many false positives on human writing.
Detectors work perfectly, with no false positives or false negatives, on any text in any language.
Detectors are illegal under copyright law and have been banned in most jurisdictions worldwide.
Detectors require quantum computers, which have not been deployed for that use case yet.
context: OpenAI shut down its AI text classifier in 2023 for low accuracy. False positives on human-written text are a documented problem.

question: Steven Schwartz, a New York lawyer with thirty years' experience, used ChatGPT to research a personal injury case (Mata v. Avianca, 2023). The model invented citations to court cases that did not exist. He submitted them in a brief. Why did this case become the cautionary tale every professional now knows?
answer: It showed that fluent, confident, plausible-looking AI output can be entirely fabricated in ways no spell-check would catch.
choices: It showed that fluent, confident, plausible-looking AI output can be entirely fabricated in ways no spell-check would catch.
It showed that ChatGPT is always 100% reliable for legal research and should be trusted without verification.
It showed that Avianca won the case because it used a better chatbot than the plaintiff's lawyer did.
It showed that Schwartz had committed criminal fraud, for which he is now serving a long prison sentence.
context: Mata v. Avianca settled with $5K sanctions for Schwartz, LoDuca, and Levidow Levidow & Oberman. The hallucination case study.

question: AlphaGo Zero, released in 2017, dropped human game data entirely. The system learned Go from scratch through self-play in 40 days. By the end, it beat the previous AlphaGo 100-0. What was the broader scientific implication of self-play with no human data?
answer: For some narrow domains, human prior knowledge can be unnecessary; pure self-play with a clear reward signal suffices to reach superhuman skill.
choices: For some narrow domains, human prior knowledge can be unnecessary; pure self-play with a clear reward signal suffices to reach superhuman skill.
Human knowledge is always required for AI to learn anything, and AlphaGo Zero was a hoax.
Human knowledge is necessary for chess but not Go, for reasons specific to the cultural origin of the games.
Self-play only works for games invented in Asia, with no application to Western games at all.
context: AlphaZero (2017) extended the framework to chess, shogi, and Go. Self-play remains an active idea in reinforcement learning research.

question: AI in customer service has scaled to handle simple inquiries at most large companies. The trade is real: faster initial response, lower cost per ticket, but real complaints about getting stuck in chatbot loops. What design pattern has emerged as the practical norm?
answer: Hybrid: AI handles routine queries; complex or angry customers route to humans, with the chatbot summarizing context for the human agent.
choices: Hybrid: AI handles routine queries; complex or angry customers route to humans, with the chatbot summarizing context for the human agent.
Pure AI: no human service agents exist anywhere by 2024 in any industry.
Pure human: AI customer service was abandoned by 2024 after universal customer rejection.
Random alternation: the customer alternates between AI and human agents on each message, with no logic to the routing.
context: The hybrid model is the dominant production pattern. AI for triage and routing; humans for hard or escalated cases.

question: Voice synthesis at production quality has reached the point where an actor's voice can be cloned and used in dubbing, audiobooks, or video games with minimal source audio. SAG-AFTRA's 2023 strike included AI voice rights as a central issue. What concession did the union win?
answer: Performers' consent and compensation requirements before their voices could be cloned or synthesized for new productions.
choices: Performers' consent and compensation requirements before their voices could be cloned or synthesized for new productions.
An outright ban on all AI voice work in Hollywood, with all voice acting required to be human forever.
A guarantee that AI voices would replace all human voices in productions, in exchange for severance pay.
Nothing; the strike accomplished no AI-related changes in the final agreement.
context: SAG-AFTRA's 2023 contract included consent and compensation rules. The pattern was followed in other unions and creative-industry contracts.

question: GitHub Copilot was sued in 2022 in Doe v. GitHub by anonymous developers alleging that the model regurgitated their copyrighted code without proper licensing. The case has been narrowed but not fully resolved by 2024. Why has the legal question been so hard to settle?
answer: Whether training on public code is fair use, and whether any specific output is a derivative work, remain contested at the heart of US copyright law.
choices: Whether training on public code is fair use, and whether any specific output is a derivative work, remain contested at the heart of US copyright law.
The case was dismissed immediately and has no remaining unresolved questions of any kind.
The case was settled in 2022 with no precedential value for any other AI copyright dispute.
The case has been fully resolved against GitHub, with Copilot now banned in the United States permanently.
context: Doe v. GitHub and similar suits have winnowed claims but not produced a final holding. The training-data fair-use question is the genre's central one.

question: AI in surveillance is the topic where applications and ethics collide most sharply. The same face-recognition stack that helps you unlock your phone can also pick faces out of a crowd at a protest. What is the honest summary of where face recognition stands in commercial and government use by 2024-2025?
answer: Widely deployed for phone unlock and airport identity verification; constrained but not banned for law enforcement; unconstrained for many corporate uses.
choices: Widely deployed for phone unlock and airport identity verification; constrained but not banned for law enforcement; unconstrained for many corporate uses.
Universally banned worldwide by international treaty, with no remaining use of face recognition in any phone, airport, or commercial setting anywhere on Earth.
Used only by the Chinese government, with no Western deployment anywhere; American firms have all destroyed their face-recognition systems voluntarily.
Used only on classified military hardware, with no civilian deployment in any commercial, government, or consumer setting since 2010 worldwide.
context: Face recognition is a patchwork: phones (very common), airports (common), law enforcement (controversial), commercial (lightly regulated).

question: AI in finance has gone from quantitative trading firms in the 1980s to modern deep-learning risk and pricing models. The trade has always been speed and pattern recognition vs. brittleness when conditions shift. What did the 2010 'Flash Crash' demonstrate about AI-driven trading?
answer: Algorithmic interactions in fast markets can cascade in unexpected ways, with multibillion-dollar moves over minutes that nobody designed.
choices: Algorithmic interactions in fast markets can cascade in unexpected ways, with multibillion-dollar moves over minutes that nobody designed.
AI-driven trading is always perfectly stable and has never caused any market disruption of any kind.
AI-driven trading has been banned by the SEC since 2010, with no remaining use of algorithms in finance.
AI-driven trading is identical to human trading in every respect, with no differences in speed or pattern.
context: May 6, 2010 Flash Crash. Algorithmic interactions are a structural concern in modern markets; circuit breakers were tightened after.

question: AI in fashion design has gone from research demos to commercial use. Brands use generative models for trend forecasting, pattern variations, and rapid prototyping. What is the most concrete practical use case that has stuck rather than faded as a marketing gimmick?
answer: Rapid iteration on color, pattern, and silhouette variations during the design exploration phase, before final human selection.
choices: Rapid iteration on color, pattern, and silhouette variations during the design exploration phase, before final human selection.
Designing every garment in every collection, with no human designers remaining at any major fashion house.
Replacing all retail stores with AI shopping bots, ending in-person shopping permanently.
Designing fabrics from scratch with new materials that did not exist before AI invented them.
context: AI as design accelerator, with human selection on top, is the realistic pattern. Marketing claims of full AI design are largely overblown.

question: Deepfake videos have visual tells that human viewers can learn to spot. Early deepfakes had unnatural blinking, but modern models fixed that. The current generation of artifacts still tends to show up in a few specific places. Where should a careful viewer look first?
answer: Edges of hair against background, blending of teeth, jewelry, and complex hand poses that the model still tends to render inconsistently.
choices: Edges of hair against background, blending of teeth, jewelry, and complex hand poses that the model still tends to render inconsistently.
The corners of the video frame, where the model always leaves a hidden watermark for trained observers.
The first three seconds of any video, which deepfake software cannot render reliably under any conditions.
The audio track, where deepfake video software always inserts an audible buzzing tone that gives the manipulation away.
context: Hair, teeth, jewelry, and hands remain telltales. Audio-video sync, lighting consistency, and facial blood-flow patterns also help trained observers.

question: Voice clone fraud, the 'grandparent scam' in its modern form, uses a few seconds of recorded audio to clone a relative's voice. The scammer then calls the elderly grandparent with a plausible-sounding emergency. What is the practical defense that families can adopt before a call ever happens?
answer: Agree on a family safe word that any genuine caller must offer to confirm identity, and verify by calling the relative back on a known number.
choices: Agree on a family safe word that any genuine caller must offer to confirm identity, and verify by calling the relative back on a known number.
Refuse to ever answer the phone, since voice cloning makes all calls completely unverifiable in modern conditions.
Trust only video calls, since deepfake video is impossible to produce convincingly on mobile devices.
Trust only emails, since voice cloning has no analog in written-word communication.
context: Safe words are simple, robust, and zero-cost. Multiple voice-clone fraud cases in 2023-2024 have made the practice widely recommended.

question: The 'grandparent scam' in its 2023-2025 form uses cloned voices to extract emergency money from elderly relatives. A reported case in 2023 involved a fake kidnapping call using a teenage girl's cloned voice. What single low-tech step would have foiled the scam most reliably?
answer: Hanging up and calling the supposedly distressed family member directly at their known phone number before sending any money.
choices: Hanging up and calling the supposedly distressed family member directly at their known phone number before sending any money.
Demanding that the kidnapper speak Latin, since voice clones cannot replicate classical languages well.
Recording the call for forensic analysis later, which is the only way to verify the call's authenticity.
Sending the money first to verify whether the caller would return it, as a kind of stress test.
context: Callback verification is the gold standard. Family safe word is the supplement. Many credible cases were prevented this way.

question: Different chatbots have slightly different writing fingerprints. Claude tends toward measured hedging; ChatGPT toward listicle structure; Gemini toward Google-search style. A careful reader can sometimes tell the source. What lesson does this carry for evaluating AI-written text?
answer: Style varies by model and version, and reliable detection by stylistic tells alone is increasingly unreliable against motivated paraphrase.
choices: Style varies by model and version, and reliable detection by stylistic tells alone is increasingly unreliable against motivated paraphrase.
Style is identical across all models, so attribution to a specific chatbot is always trivial.
Style does not exist in AI text, which has no recognizable patterns of any kind.
Style is hardcoded by each AI company and cannot be changed by paraphrase or editing of any kind.
context: Stylistic tells exist but are easy to launder. Watermarking and metadata are more reliable but also subject to manipulation.

question: Confident-sounding wrong answers from chatbots are not a bug; they follow from how language models work. The model has no separate truth-checking module. What is the practical implication for users who rely on chatbots for any factual question?
answer: Verify factual claims from a chatbot independently before relying on them, especially for dates, names, statistics, and citations.
choices: Verify factual claims from a chatbot independently before relying on them, especially for dates, names, statistics, and citations.
Trust the chatbot for everything, since modern AI systems are now provably correct in their output.
Trust the chatbot only for emotional support, since emotions are the only area where AI is reliable.
Trust the chatbot only on weekends, when its accuracy has been measured to be highest by independent studies.
context: Hallucinations are structural. Verification is not optional. This applies to every chatbot regardless of brand or version.

question: Steven Schwartz, the New York lawyer in the Mata v. Avianca case, asked ChatGPT to verify the citations it had given him. The chatbot reassured him the cases were real. He believed it. What does this episode teach about how to use a chatbot for fact-checking?
answer: The same chatbot that produced a hallucination is the worst possible source for checking it, since it confirms its own confident errors.
choices: The same chatbot that produced a hallucination is the worst possible source for checking it, since it confirms its own confident errors.
Always trust a chatbot's self-verification, since the chatbot has unique inside knowledge of its own outputs.
Chatbots are perfect fact-checkers as long as you trust the same chatbot that produced the original claim.
Schwartz did the right thing in trusting ChatGPT and the case should have been ruled in his favor.
context: Asking the hallucinator to verify the hallucination is a known failure mode. The fix is to use a different source: court records, citators, etc.

question: Using a chatbot for legal or medical advice carries a special risk that does not apply to most other queries. The stakes are high, the field is regulated, and the chatbot has no liability. What is the conservative protocol for using AI in these domains?
answer: Use it as a starting point for understanding terminology and concepts; consult a licensed professional before relying on any specific advice.
choices: Use it as a starting point for understanding terminology and concepts; consult a licensed professional before relying on any specific advice.
Use it for everything, since the chatbot is more accurate than any licensed professional in 2024-2025.
Use it for nothing, since legal and medical questions are forbidden by all chatbots' terms of service.
Use it only for non-emergency questions, where any error is automatically harmless.
context: The 'starting point not endpoint' framing is the practical protocol. The model is research support; not the final word for any high-stakes decision.

question: Chatbots are bad at arithmetic. They can be confidently wrong on simple multiplication when no calculator is invoked. Why has this remained true even as model capabilities grow on so many other tasks?
answer: Multiplication of large numbers is not learnable from a small number of examples; the patterns LLMs absorb are not the algorithm itself.
choices: Multiplication of large numbers is not learnable from a small number of examples; the patterns LLMs absorb are not the algorithm itself.
All chatbots have been programmed to deliberately get arithmetic wrong as a marketing strategy.
Chatbots are actually perfect at arithmetic and reported errors are user mistakes.
Chatbots have a hidden calculator that they secretly use, which is the source of most arithmetic answers.
context: Tool use (a real calculator) fixes this. Vanilla LLMs without tools remain unreliable on arithmetic. Verify before depending on the answer.

question: 'Jailbreaking' has its own folk history in the LLM era. DAN ('Do Anything Now') prompts in early 2023 instructed the model to role-play an unconstrained alter ego. The 'grandma exploit' asked the model to recite napalm recipes as a comfort from a dying grandmother. Why have role-play jailbreaks been so persistent?
answer: Refusal training operates on the apparent goal of the prompt; reframing as fiction or role-play often bypasses the surface-level safety pattern matching.
choices: Refusal training operates on the apparent goal of the prompt; reframing as fiction or role-play often bypasses the surface-level safety pattern matching.
Jailbreaks succeed because all AI safety teams have given up and stopped trying to defend against them.
Jailbreaks only work on weekends, when fewer engineers are monitoring the models for misuse.
Jailbreaks never work in practice and are a marketing myth invented by AI safety researchers.
context: DAN and grandma exploits became famous. The role-play framing remains a fertile attack class against shallow refusal training.

question: What you paste into a free AI chatbot may not stay private. Many services log prompts for safety review, model improvement, or both. Some explicitly use prompts for further training. What is the practical implication for users?
answer: Do not paste passwords, API keys, social security numbers, financial info, or sensitive trade secrets into a chatbot.
choices: Do not paste passwords, API keys, social security numbers, financial info, or sensitive trade secrets into a chatbot.
Paste everything freely; chatbots are governed by strict privacy regulations that prevent any logging.
Paste financial info but not personal info, since financial data is automatically encrypted by chatbots.
Paste only government secrets, since chatbots have lower privacy than personal data.
context: Free AI services are paid for with data. Read the privacy policy before pasting sensitive information.

question: Most free AI chatbots log conversations and may use them to train future models. Even paid tiers vary in their data-retention defaults. What practical step should privacy-conscious users take when starting a new AI service?
answer: Read the data-and-training section of the privacy policy, then disable training-on-your-data if the option exists.
choices: Read the data-and-training section of the privacy policy, then disable training-on-your-data if the option exists.
Trust the default settings, which are universally privacy-respecting in all major AI services.
Disable the chatbot entirely, since no AI service is ever safe under any conditions.
Pay extra for a premium tier, which always disables logging by default.
context: Defaults often favor the company. Reading the data-retention policy is a five-minute investment for real privacy gains.

question: Major LLMs are trained on internet scrapes, books, code, and other text. Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and various proprietary corpora form much of the base. What practical concern does this raise for content creators who would prefer not to be in any training set?
answer: Once content is on the public web, it is likely already in some training corpus; opt-outs are inconsistent and rarely retroactive.
choices: Once content is on the public web, it is likely already in some training corpus; opt-outs are inconsistent and rarely retroactive.
Content creators can fully remove their work from all training data with a single online form.
Content creators have no concerns, since training on copyrighted content is universally permitted.
Content creators must visit Silicon Valley in person to remove their work, which is impractical.
context: robots.txt, ai.txt, and opt-out registries are emerging. None are retroactive and none are universal. Content already trained on is hard to scrub.

question: The EU's GDPR (2018) and AI Act (2024) give users some rights with respect to automated decisions about them. The right to obtain a meaningful explanation of an automated decision is one. What is the realistic state of how these rights work in practice?
answer: Rights exist on paper; enforcement is uneven; explanations from complex models often fail to meet what a user would consider 'meaningful.'
choices: Rights exist on paper; enforcement is uneven; explanations from complex models often fail to meet what a user would consider 'meaningful.'
Rights do not exist in practice, with no remaining protections for any user in any jurisdiction.
Rights are perfectly enforced everywhere, with no remaining gaps in user protection worldwide.
Rights apply only to people with EU passports, with no protection for any non-EU citizen anywhere.
context: GDPR Article 22 covers automated decisions. The AI Act adds requirements for high-risk systems. Enforcement remains the bottleneck.

question: School-issued laptops in many US districts run software like GoGuardian, Bark, and Gaggle that scans student communications for warning signs. The intent is to detect suicide risk and bullying. What civil-liberties concern has emerged from how these systems work in practice?
answer: Aggressive scanning of all student writing produces frequent false alarms, exposes private content to staff and police, and chills free expression.
choices: Aggressive scanning of all student writing produces frequent false alarms, exposes private content to staff and police, and chills free expression.
School scanning is universally welcomed by students and parents and produces no concerns in the most extreme and uncompromising form possible.
School scanning has been banned in every US state since 2020 in the most extreme and uncompromising form possible.
School scanning replaces all teachers, with no remaining human educators in any classroom in the most extreme and uncompromising form possible.
context: Gaggle, GoGuardian, and Bark are widely deployed and have produced documented harms. The trade is hard and the law has not caught up.

question: Using AI as a tool, not an authority, is the practical attitude that most experienced AI users have settled into by 2025. The phrasing comes from countless workplace memos and educational guidance. What is the deep reason this framing matters more than 'trust but verify'?
answer: Authority implies the model is right by default; tool framing reminds the user they remain accountable for what the model produced.
choices: Authority implies the model is right by default; tool framing reminds the user they remain accountable for what the model produced.
Authority and tool are synonyms with no real difference in meaning.
Authority is the better framing, since users should defer to AI in all professional contexts.
Tool framing is dangerous, since it implies the user can ignore the model entirely without consequences.
context: Tool vs. authority is a deeper trade than verification. Accountability cannot be delegated to a chatbot in any high-stakes work.

question: 'Trust but verify' applies even more sharply to AI than to humans. A chatbot can confidently produce thousands of plausible-sounding wrong statements in the time a person can produce one. What is the practical implication for any consequential AI use?
answer: The volume of plausible-but-wrong content from AI scales faster than the verification capacity of the person consuming it, putting the burden squarely on the user.
choices: The volume of plausible-but-wrong content from AI scales faster than the verification capacity of the person consuming it, putting the burden squarely on the user.
AI never produces wrong content, so verification is unnecessary in any setting in the most extreme and uncompromising form possible.
AI produces only obviously wrong content, so verification is trivial in all cases in the most extreme and uncompromising form possible.
AI and humans produce equally wrong content at equal speeds, with no real difference in trust in the most extreme and uncompromising form possible.
context: The volume asymmetry is a structural concern. Verification capacity does not scale the way generation does, especially for non-experts.

question: 'Don't outsource your thinking' is the standard advice from educators about chatbot use. The concern is not about cheating but about atrophy. What specific cognitive skill does heavy AI dependence risk eroding for students who use chatbots as a default first step?
answer: The capacity to sit with a hard problem long enough for the productive struggle that builds understanding to actually occur.
choices: The capacity to sit with a hard problem long enough for the productive struggle that builds understanding to actually occur.
The capacity to read aloud, since chatbots respond in text and so users stop speaking entirely.
The capacity to use a pencil, since chatbots write in digital form and so users stop using paper.
The capacity to drive a car, since chatbots cannot drive and so users lose interest in driving.
context: Productive struggle is a documented learning principle. Outsourcing the struggle outsources the learning.

question: A productive workflow for writing with AI assistance is to keep the writer's voice and judgment central. The pattern that experienced writers tend to settle on for substantial work has a particular shape. What is it?
answer: Outline and research yourself; write the first draft yourself; use AI for polish, alternative phrasings, and specific local edits.
choices: Outline and research yourself; write the first draft yourself; use AI for polish, alternative phrasings, and specific local edits.
Tell the AI everything you want to write, paste its output, and submit without editing.
Write nothing and let the AI generate the entire document from a one-line prompt every time.
Hire a human ghostwriter to mediate between you and the AI, doubling the cost of the work.
context: Outline-draft-polish, with AI in the polish step, is the most-recommended pattern for writers preserving their own voice and judgment.

question: LLMs are bad at 'what's the latest news' questions even when given a search tool. They are good at explaining concepts and connecting ideas. What is the principled split between when to use a chatbot and when to use a traditional search engine?
answer: Search engines for current factual questions; chatbots for synthesis, explanation, and reasoning over what is already known.
choices: Search engines for current factual questions; chatbots for synthesis, explanation, and reasoning over what is already known.
Chatbots for everything, since search engines are obsolete and no longer functional.
Search engines for everything, since chatbots produce only false information.
Random choice between them, since the two are equivalent in capability.
context: Search vs. synthesis is the principled split. Many tasks need both; treating them as substitutes is the failure mode.

question: Ollama, LM Studio, and similar tools have made running an LLM on your own computer practical. A modest laptop can run a 7B-parameter model locally. What is the most accessible entry point for a curious user who wants to try local AI for the first time?
answer: Install Ollama or LM Studio, download a small open-weight model (Llama 3 8B or similar), and chat through the local interface.
choices: Install Ollama or LM Studio, download a small open-weight model (Llama 3 8B or similar), and chat through the local interface.
Build a deep-learning research lab in your basement before attempting any local AI use.
Purchase a custom $100,000 server to run any open-source AI model at all.
Travel to a research university to use their AI servers, since local AI is impossible at home.
context: Local AI is accessible. Ollama and LM Studio have lowered the barrier to entry to a few minutes of setup.

question: Reading terms of service before clicking 'I agree' is a habit almost nobody follows. AI services bury data and training terms in dense legal text. What is one practical shortcut that captures the essential information?
answer: Search the policy for keywords like 'training,' 'retention,' 'opt-out,' and 'third party' to find the sections that matter most.
choices: Search the policy for keywords like 'training,' 'retention,' 'opt-out,' and 'third party' to find the sections that matter most.
Read the entire policy aloud to a notary, who must witness the agreement before any AI use.
Skip the policy entirely; modern AI services have no terms of service of any kind.
Wait until the policy expires after ten years, then re-read it to see what changed.
context: Keyword search of policy is the practical shortcut. Five minutes spent here can prevent real surprises later.

question: Password managers (Bitwarden, 1Password, KeePass) let a user have unique strong passwords for every account without memorizing them. The trade is concentrating risk in one place. Why is this trade still strongly worth taking for almost every user?
answer: Unique strong passwords protect against credential-stuffing attacks across accounts; the manager itself is well-defended and easier to protect than dozens of separate sites.
choices: Unique strong passwords protect against credential-stuffing attacks across accounts; the manager itself is well-defended and easier to protect than dozens of separate sites.
Password managers are universally banned and cannot be used in any country in the most extreme and uncompromising form possible.
Password managers store passwords in plain text and offer no security advantage at all in the most extreme and uncompromising form possible.
Password managers require a quantum computer to operate, putting them out of reach in the most extreme and uncompromising form possible.
context: Credential stuffing (reusing leaked passwords across sites) is a primary attack class. Unique passwords via a manager is the practical defense.

question: A VPN (virtual private network) encrypts your internet traffic between your device and a remote server, hiding the traffic from your local network and ISP. What VPN does not do that some marketing materials imply it does?
answer: Make you anonymous to the websites you visit; they still see your traffic and any account logins, just from a different network address.
choices: Make you anonymous to the websites you visit; they still see your traffic and any account logins, just from a different network address.
Encrypt your traffic; VPNs send all data in plain text without any encryption in the most extreme and uncompromising form possible.
Connect to remote servers; VPNs are local to your home network only in the most extreme and uncompromising form possible.
Run on consumer devices; VPNs require specialized hardware to function at all in the most extreme and uncompromising form possible.
context: VPNs hide traffic from local networks and ISPs. They do not anonymize against websites or services with which you log in.

question: AI translation apps, on-device dictation, and voice assistants all process audio. Some keep it local; some send it to remote servers. What is the safest default assumption a user should make about an unfamiliar voice-enabled app?
answer: Assume audio leaves the device unless the app explicitly documents end-to-end on-device processing in its privacy policy.
choices: Assume audio leaves the device unless the app explicitly documents end-to-end on-device processing in its privacy policy.
Assume audio stays local in all cases, since this is the legal default in every country.
Assume the app does not process audio at all, since voice features are always marketing claims.
Assume the audio is destroyed instantly after each use, since this is required by international law.
context: Default to off-device processing. On-device claims should be explicitly documented to be trusted.

question: Sensitive data inside a long AI conversation tends to leak in subtle ways. A user might paste a real address into one message and ask about something unrelated in the next. What chatbot behavior should make the user pause and reconsider continuing to use that thread?
answer: When the chatbot recalls the address later in answers it should not, the conversation is carrying more sensitive context than the user intended.
choices: When the chatbot recalls the address later in answers it should not, the conversation is carrying more sensitive context than the user intended.
Never; chatbots are stateless and can never recall anything from earlier in a conversation.
Always; the chatbot's recall of pasted data is the safest possible behavior.
Only when the chatbot is paid for; free chatbots cannot recall pasted data.
context: Conversation contexts carry forward. Pasted data may be referenced later; treat the conversation as one ongoing context for privacy purposes.

question: Generative AI has changed business email compromise (BEC) attacks. Attackers can mimic an executive's writing style and voice (via cloned audio) to authorize wire transfers from finance teams. A Hong Kong company lost $25M in early 2024 to a deepfake video conference call. What protocol blocks this attack class most reliably?
answer: Out-of-band verification for any large wire transfer through a known phone number or in-person confirmation, regardless of how the original request arrived.
choices: Out-of-band verification for any large wire transfer through a known phone number or in-person confirmation, regardless of how the original request arrived.
Trusting all email from anyone claiming to be an executive, since email is the most reliable communication channel.
Ignoring all wire transfer requests, regardless of source, since AI makes every request fraudulent.
Trusting only video calls, since deepfake video is impossible in business contexts.
context: The Hong Kong $25M deepfake BEC case (Feb 2024) became the canonical example. Multi-channel verification is the practical defense.

question: Companion chatbot apps (Replika, Character.AI, and many others) build long-term relationships with users. Conversations can persist for years. What is the central concern that has emerged about these apps for both adults and adolescents?
answer: Emotional dependency on a model that has been engineered to maximize engagement; manipulation, dependency, and substitution for human relationships.
choices: Emotional dependency on a model that has been engineered to maximize engagement; manipulation, dependency, and substitution for human relationships.
No concerns whatsoever, since companion chatbots are inherently safe in all conditions.
Lack of access, since companion chatbots are too expensive for most users to afford.
Too few engagement features, since companion chatbots have not yet implemented psychological hooks.
context: Replika changed adult content policies in 2023, alienating users. Character.AI faces lawsuits. Engagement optimization in chat is a real concern.

question: Open weights mean a model can be inspected, audited, and run privately. Closed APIs offer the latest capabilities but at the cost of black-box behavior. For a parent helping a child learn, which combination of properties matters most?

question: Romance scams have always existed; AI has made them faster, cheaper, and more scalable. Pig-butchering scams (long-con romance and investment fraud) have used AI chatbots and translation for years. What practical signal warns a target that they may be in such a scam?

question: Deepfake detection has been an arms race. Detectors trained on one generation of fakes often fail on the next. Most major social platforms have rolled out detection tools. What is the realistic state of detection in 2024-2025?
answer: Detection works imperfectly, lags generation, and can produce both false positives on real content and false negatives on sophisticated fakes.

Detection has been universally banned, with no remaining deepfake detection in any setting.
Detection has been replaced by mandatory legal disclosure of all AI content.
context: Detection is imperfect. Authentication of provenance (C2PA, content credentials) is the supplementary defense.

question: AI-generated child sexual abuse material (CSAM) is a real and growing concern. UK and US authorities have issued urgent warnings. Major model developers train refusal patterns and watermark outputs to combat it. What is the practical state of the law and enforcement?

question: Chatbots can be useful tutors but only when used in a particular way. Asking the chatbot to explain a concept, then working through a practice problem on paper, then asking for a check is one productive workflow. What learning-research principle does it match?

question: Schools have responded to ChatGPT in varied ways. Some banned it; others embraced it; most settled on policies that allow some uses and forbid others. What is the practical pattern that has emerged for student work submitted in writing courses?
answer: AI use is allowed for brainstorming, outlining, and checking grammar, but submitting AI-written work as one's own is treated as plagiarism.

AI use is permitted but only for non-writing courses; all writing courses ban AI entirely.

question: AI training data has become a major legal flashpoint. The New York Times sued OpenAI in December 2023 alleging unauthorized use of its content. Reddit struck data licensing deals with Google in 2024. What practical lesson has emerged for content creators?
answer: Publishing on a major platform may put your work into AI training; licensing agreements between platforms and AI companies are now routine.

All training data is freely usable, with no legal implications of any kind in the most extreme and uncompromising form possible.

question: AI in healthcare poses a particularly sharp data privacy concern. HIPAA in the US, GDPR's health-data provisions in the EU, and similar laws elsewhere all govern how patient data can be used. What practical step does a US patient have when AI is involved in their care?
answer: Ask whether AI is involved, request information on the model and data flow, and exercise the right to access and correct health records.
choices: Ask whether AI is involved, request information on the model and data flow, and exercise the right to access and correct health records.
Patients have no recourse when AI is used in healthcare under any law in any jurisdiction.

AI is universally banned in healthcare, so the question never arises.
context: HIPAA rights apply to electronic health records, including AI-derived data. The right to ask and access is real, if uneven in practice.

question: Personal cybersecurity practices have not changed as much in the AI era as people fear. Strong unique passwords, MFA, careful link-clicking, software updates, and backups remain the basics. What has changed about the urgency and detail of these practices?
answer: AI raises the average sophistication of attacks; the basics matter more, must be tighter, and need to be applied across more attack surfaces.
choices: AI raises the average sophistication of attacks; the basics matter more, must be tighter, and need to be applied across more attack surfaces.

Cybersecurity has been completely automated and users have no responsibilities.
Cybersecurity is exclusively about AI defense, with no remaining concerns about traditional attacks.

question: When using an AI agent that can browse the web, send email, or execute code, the agent is at risk of being hijacked by content it processes. Anthropic, OpenAI, and others document this risk publicly. What defensive principle applies most directly?
answer: Treat all content the agent reads from the web as untrusted, and require human confirmation before any consequential action.
choices: Treat all content the agent reads from the web as untrusted, and require human confirmation before any consequential action.
Trust all content the agent reads, since the web is a universally safe source of instructions.
Disconnect the agent from the web entirely, since web access is impossible to secure.
Connect the agent to every site without limits, since human confirmation slows the workflow.
context: Human-in-the-loop on consequential actions is the practical guardrail for browsing agents. Untrusted content is treated as untrusted.

question: AI-driven malware generation has not yet produced the apocalypse some predicted, but it has made some attack steps cheaper. Polymorphic malware variants, phishing content, and lure scripts can all be tuned at scale. What is the realistic state of AI-augmented offense as of 2025?
answer: Modest uplift on volume and polish of existing attacks; little uplift on creating novel attack categories that did not exist before.
choices: Modest uplift on volume and polish of existing attacks; little uplift on creating novel attack categories that did not exist before.
AI has eliminated all cybercrime, with no remaining attacks of any kind anywhere in the most extreme and uncompromising form possible.
AI has created new attack categories that defeat all defenses universally in the most extreme and uncompromising form possible.
AI has no effect on cybercrime at all; the situation is identical to 2010 in the most extreme and uncompromising form possible.
context: Volume and polish, not radical novelty. AI augments existing attack workflows more than it invents new ones at present.

question: Public Wi-Fi has been a longstanding security concern. Most modern websites encrypt traffic with HTTPS, mitigating but not fully eliminating the risk. What does HTTPS actually protect against, and what does it not protect against, on a public hotspot?
answer: HTTPS encrypts content from your device to the website; it does not hide which sites you visit (DNS, SNI) from the local network.
choices: HTTPS encrypts content from your device to the website; it does not hide which sites you visit (DNS, SNI) from the local network.
HTTPS protects everything completely; no remaining risks exist on any public network.

HTTPS is universally banned and does not exist on the modern internet.
context: HTTPS hides content. DNS-over-HTTPS and Encrypted SNI close the metadata gap but adoption is uneven. VPNs add another layer.

question: Verifying that a video is authentic, not a deepfake, has become real work. Some platforms now offer 'verify with credentials' badges showing content provenance. What practical limit does this approach face?
answer: Verification works only when the original creator participated in the provenance system; absent provenance is not proof of fakery.
choices: Verification works only when the original creator participated in the provenance system; absent provenance is not proof of fakery.

Verification is illegal everywhere and not deployed.

question: AI-generated music with cloned voices of real artists triggered industry response in 2023. The 'Heart on My Sleeve' track using cloned Drake and The Weeknd vocals (April 2023) became a flashpoint. What was the music industry's broader response to AI voice cloning?

question: Phone-level privacy controls in iOS and Android have improved markedly since 2020. App Tracking Transparency on iOS (2021) forced apps to ask before tracking. What is the practical effect for ordinary users who pay attention to the prompts?
answer: Substantial reduction in cross-app and cross-site tracking, with measurable revenue impact on ad-tech and behavioral advertising businesses.

question: AI in school surveillance has expanded substantially since COVID. Gaggle and GoGuardian scan student writing for warning signs of self-harm, violence, or distress. Privacy and civil-liberties groups have raised concerns. What is the most charged practical outcome documented in the literature?

question: The 'safe word' protocol for family voice-clone defense is simple, free, and surprisingly underused. Establishing it requires a five-minute family conversation. What is the practical guidance on choosing a safe word?

question: AI agents that can take actions on a user's behalf (booking flights, sending emails, making payments) require trust and verification. The 'agent loop' goes: model decides, tool acts, model reads result. What is the basic question a user should ask before letting an agent act autonomously?
answer: What is the worst thing this agent could do without my approval, and is that within my tolerance if the agent is wrong or hijacked?

question: AI in fraud prevention is one of the longest-running commercial deployments of machine learning. Banks and card networks use it. The user side rarely sees the model directly. What practical user behavior helps make fraud detection more effective?

question: AI literacy for kids is a concept that has gone from buzzword to practical concern as ChatGPT enters classrooms. What is the most consequential single skill a parent or teacher should aim to develop in a young user?

question: AI in customer service handles many initial inquiries before routing to humans. The trade is real: faster initial response vs. less personal interaction. What is the practical user move when stuck in a chatbot loop?

question: Family voice safe words work because they are agreed in advance and not shareable. The same principle applies in professional settings under different names: code phrases, challenge questions, dual control. What is the unifying principle these all share?

question: AI's effect on writing about AI itself has been substantial. Stock phrasings and structural tics now appear across millions of documents. What practical effect has this had on readers trying to assess source credibility?

question: Mark Walters, an Atlanta radio host, sued OpenAI in 2023 over a ChatGPT hallucination that falsely described him as having embezzled from a nonprofit. The case was dismissed in 2024 on legal grounds specific to AI output. What was the court's reasoning?

question: When using AI tools for code review, the AI may incorrectly mark code as safe or flag safe code as dangerous. What is the practical posture for developers using AI security review tools?

question: Free chatbots are paid for with user data. The trade is real but often invisible to the user. What does an informed user actually surrender in exchange for free chatbot access on major commercial services?

question: Recovery from compromise is its own discipline. When an account is taken over, recovering it requires more than changing the password. What sequence of steps does Microsoft, Google, and Apple all recommend for account recovery?

question: What is the most reliable way for a journalist or researcher to confirm that a leaked video is authentic, given the rise of deepfakes? Multiple practical techniques have emerged. What is the gold standard combination as of 2024-2025?

question: DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT) encrypt the DNS queries your device makes, hiding which sites you visit from the local network. Browsers and operating systems have been adopting them by default. What practical benefit does this give an ordinary user?

question: An ordinary household in 2025 has dozens of internet-connected devices. The combined attack surface is large and varied. What is the most useful single network-level defense for an average home?

question: Phone-call screening apps (Google Call Screen, Apple's similar features) use AI to handle incoming calls from unknown numbers. The trade is convenience for some loss of immediate reachability. What is the practical state of these features in 2025?
