question: An AI generates a song that sounds like a famous singer. The singer never recorded it. What is happening?
answer: Voice cloning made a fake song
choices: Voice cloning made a fake song
The singer secretly recorded it
The radio mailed it to them
The singer was born twice
context: Voice-cloning AI can copy a singer's voice from just a few clips. Real artists often dislike this.

question: Two kids see a clip showing a teacher saying something rude. The teacher denies it. What's a good first step?
answer: Ask a grown-up to help check it
choices: Ask a grown-up to help check it
Send the clip to the whole school
Believe the clip and stay mad
Print copies for every locker
context: Adults can help track down whether a clip is real, edited, or fully made up by AI.

question: A computer learns to spot cats by looking at many cat photos. What are those photos called?
answer: Training data
choices: Training data
Counting beads
Reading shelves
Painting paper
context: AI learns from examples called training data. More good examples usually means smarter behavior.

question: An AI is trained on only dog pictures, then shown a cat. What is likely to happen?
answer: It guesses 'dog' since that's all it knew
choices: It guesses 'dog' since that's all it knew
It writes a poem about cats
It calls its programmer fast
It paints the cat orange
context: AI knows what it has seen. Show it only dogs, and even a cat looks like a dog to it.

question: Your puppy learns 'sit' from many treats and tries. What does AI 'practice' usually look like?
answer: Many examples shown over and over
choices: Many examples shown over and over
One photo seen one time only
Reading a book about sitting
Watching one movie about dogs
context: Like dogs, AI learns by repeating examples. One look usually isn't enough.

question: A team trains an AI to spot apples. They use 10 photos. The AI is bad. What is the likely fix?
answer: Use many more apple photos
choices: Use many more apple photos
Use fewer photos than 10
Use only black-and-white photos
Use pictures of bananas instead
context: Tiny datasets give weak AI. More good examples usually means a much better helper.

question: Your school wants to train an AI to read kid handwriting. Whose handwriting should be in the training photos?
answer: Lots of different kids' writing
choices: Lots of different kids' writing
Just one neat adult's letters
Only words from one country
Only words written in red
context: Many kinds of examples teach the AI to handle the real world, not just one neat style.

question: An AI grader was trained on only essays from one class. Why might it grade other classes unfairly?
answer: It only knows that one class's style
choices: It only knows that one class's style
It only works after school ends
It only likes essays in blue ink
It only reads in bright sunlight
context: Training narrowly leads to narrow skill. The AI is great on what it saw and clumsy on what it didn't.

question: Your friend says 'computers don't make mistakes.' Is this true?
answer: No, they copy mistakes in the data
choices: No, they copy mistakes in the data
Yes, computers are always right
Yes, but only on weekdays
Yes, except on space stations
context: AI learns from data. Bad or one-sided data leads to mistakes the AI happily repeats.

question: A kind of AI learns from photos that include a label, like 'cat' or 'dog.' What are those labels for?
answer: To tell the AI the right answer
choices: To tell the AI the right answer
To send the photo a birthday card
To color the photo all red
To rename the photo each month
context: Labels are like answer keys. They tell the AI which photo is which during practice.

question: Long ago, a smart man named Turing asked 'can a machine think?' Why is this a famous question?
answer: It started people thinking about AI
choices: It started people thinking about AI
It is on every birthday card
It told time on old clocks
It hid in old library books
context: Alan Turing's question helped launch the whole field of AI back in the 1950s.

question: A famous test asks: can you tell whether a chat partner is a person or a computer? Who is this test named after?
answer: Alan Turing
choices: Alan Turing
Albert Einstein
Marie Curie
Charles Darwin
context: The Turing test is a thought test for AI: if you can't tell a bot from a person in chat, the bot is impressive.

question: Years ago, a big chess computer beat the world champion. What is the lesson kids might take from that?
answer: Computers can be great at games
choices: Computers can be great at games
Chess is now a banned sport
Only grown-ups should play chess
Chess pieces eat tiny crackers
context: In 1997, IBM's Deep Blue beat the world chess champion. Game-playing AI has only grown from there.

question: Your school history book mentions AI from the 1950s. Were those AIs anything like ChatGPT?
answer: No, they were tiny and simple
choices: No, they were tiny and simple
Yes, they were even smarter
Yes, they wrote love poems
Yes, but only in Spanish
context: Old AI was tiny and rule-based. Modern chatbots came from huge models trained in the 2010s and after.

question: AI had quiet years called 'AI winters.' What does 'AI winter' mean in plain words?
answer: Times when AI funding froze up
choices: Times when AI funding froze up
Cold months in north Alaska
The names of robot dogs there
Tests robots take in cold rooms
context: Funding for AI dropped during certain decades when results didn't match promises. Then progress resumed.

question: An old chatbot from 1966 was named ELIZA and pretended to be a counselor. Why is it famous?
answer: It was one of the first chatbots
choices: It was one of the first chatbots
It went to a real college
It got a job at a hotel
It wrote a song with Elvis
context: ELIZA used simple pattern matching. People still felt heard by it, which surprised researchers.

question: AI from the 1970s tried to copy 'expert' workers like doctors. These were called expert systems. How did they decide things?
answer: By following hand-written rules
choices: By following hand-written rules
By rolling tiny dice in jars
By smelling each patient slowly
By napping under fluorescent lights
context: Expert systems used 'if X then Y' rules built by humans. They worked in narrow areas but were brittle.

question: In 2016, a Go-playing AI named AlphaGo beat the world's best player. Why is Go a hard game for computers?
answer: Way more moves than chess to think about
choices: Way more moves than chess to think about
The board is too round to read
The pieces hide on each turn
Players are not allowed to talk
context: Go has more possible moves than chess, so older AI struggled. AlphaGo's win was a big AI moment.

question: A chatbot writes a poem one word at a time. What is it choosing each time?
answer: The most likely next word
choices: The most likely next word
A random word from the wind
A song lyric from radio
A word that rhymes with you
context: Chatbots pick the next word based on what's most likely after the words before. Repeat thousands of times.

question: You type 'Tell me a story about a duck' to a chatbot. It writes a story. Did the chatbot know about ducks before you asked?
answer: Yes, from lots of training text
choices: Yes, from lots of training text
No, it learned right now
Yes, from one duck friend
No, it asked a passing dog
context: Chatbots learn from huge piles of training text before you ever see them. They already 'know' a lot.

question: A chatbot is asked the same question twice. The answers differ slightly. Why?
answer: Some randomness is built in
choices: Some randomness is built in
It forgot the first reply
It got cold between answers
It is angry at the keyboard
context: Chatbots add randomness on purpose so answers feel fresh. The same prompt may give different replies.

question: Your sister types 'thanks' to a chatbot. The chatbot says 'You're welcome.' Did the bot feel her thanks?
answer: No, the bot only matches patterns
choices: No, the bot only matches patterns
Yes, it felt warm and fuzzy
Yes, it noted it in its diary
Yes, the bot now likes her
context: Chatbots have no feelings. They predict polite reply words because that's the pattern in training data.

question: A chatbot finishes a paragraph for you. It does not check anything in books or on the web. How can that be?
answer: Many bots write only from training data
choices: Many bots write only from training data
All bots check the library first
Bots only write while reading the news
Bots email librarians for the words
context: Plain LLM chatbots write from what they learned in training. They may or may not have web access.

question: Your phone's helper bot keeps the chat short. What is the very first word it sees from you called?
answer: Part of your prompt
choices: Part of your prompt
A part of the song
A type of food
A weather report
context: The prompt is your message. The bot reads it and decides what to write next.

question: Your homework bot tells you that George Washington flew a helicopter. That is false. What is this kind of mistake often called?
answer: A hallucination
choices: A hallucination
A celebration
A meditation
A vacation
context: When chatbots write confident but false answers, people call it a 'hallucination.' Always check facts.

question: Your sibling asks 'is the chatbot reading my homework as I type?' What might be true?
answer: Yes, the company often sees the chat
choices: Yes, the company often sees the chat
No, nothing is sent to anyone
Yes, the FBI watches each word
No, the bot reads in secret only
context: Most chatbots send chats to a company server. Treat what you type as if a stranger could read it.

question: A 'model' in AI is just a name for what?
answer: The thing that learned from the data
choices: The thing that learned from the data
A photo of someone famous
A small toy car or plane
A car-show person on stage
context: In AI, the model is the trained thing that makes guesses. Different topic from runway or toy models.

question: Your friend gave you 100 pictures of fruit, all labeled. You teach a program to spot apples. What kind of learning is this?
answer: Learning with examples and labels
choices: Learning with examples and labels
Learning by sleeping deeply
Learning by guessing only
Learning while running fast
context: When examples come with labels, AI learns the pairs. That's the most common kind of learning.

question: An AI agent learns to play a video game by getting points for good moves. What kind of training is that?
answer: Learning from rewards
choices: Learning from rewards
Learning by reading book
Learning from drawing alone
Learning by skipping a turn
context: When AI gets rewards for good actions, we call it reinforcement learning. Think 'treat for sitting.'

question: A program sorts a pile of photos with no labels at all into groups by color. What did the program do?
answer: It found a pattern on its own
choices: It found a pattern on its own
It read a book on color first
It called a kid to help out
It used a paint brush itself
context: Sorting without labels is unsupervised learning: the program finds patterns by itself.

question: A model that does great in practice but flops in real life learned the practice too well. What word describes this?
answer: Overfitting
choices: Overfitting
Underbaking
Sidewinding
Backflipping
context: Overfit models memorize practice answers and miss real-world cases. The cure is more varied examples.

question: Your math model is wrong almost every time. The fix is rarely 'add more knobs.' What is usually the real fix?
answer: Better and more varied examples
choices: Better and more varied examples
Adding more wrong answers
Drawing the model in red
Spinning the computer twice
context: Most weak AI is weak because of weak data, not weak knobs. Better examples beats fancy tricks.

question: An AI 'predicts' your next chess move. What is a prediction?
answer: A best guess from past data
choices: A best guess from past data
A song stuck on repeat
A homework worksheet
A wish made at midnight
context: Predictions are guesses based on patterns. They can be very good, but they can also be wrong.

question: Your prediction was wrong. The model 'updates.' What does that mean in plain words?
answer: It changes a little to do better
choices: It changes a little to do better
It runs away from you fast
It folds itself into a box
It hides under your bed
context: Updating tweaks the model based on the mistake so it does better the next time.

question: A friend asks an AI for help making something dangerous. The AI refuses. Why does it refuse?
answer: The makers built in safety rules
choices: The makers built in safety rules
It does not feel like answering
It is busy with another chat
It hates the color of the room
context: AI companies add safety rules so models refuse to help with dangerous tasks.

question: Your dad says 'the AI should help, but only with safe things.' What is that idea called?
answer: Safety guardrails
choices: Safety guardrails
Sleeping pillows
Quiet hours
Saving money
context: Guardrails are the rules and filters that try to keep AI helpful and away from harm.

question: Why do AI makers test new models before letting the public use them?
answer: To catch unsafe answers first
choices: To catch unsafe answers first
To learn nothing new about it
To save batteries forever
To prove it has feelings too
context: Testing finds dangerous or biased answers so the makers can fix them before launch.

question: A kind of test where humans try to break the AI on purpose is called?
answer: Red-team testing
choices: Red-team testing
Red socks contest
Red juice party
Red shoe race
context: Red-team testers act like attackers, trying to make the AI behave badly so it can be patched.

question: A chatbot answers 'I can't help with that' to a dangerous request. Should you be glad?
answer: Yes, the safety rules worked
choices: Yes, the safety rules worked
No, the bot is being rude
No, it should always answer
Yes, you can ask twice now
context: Refusals are a sign the safety rules caught a risky ask. It is the bot doing what it should.

question: Your friend wants to trick a chatbot to break its rules. What is the wise thing to do?
answer: Don't try to break it on purpose
choices: Don't try to break it on purpose
Try every trick until it works
Yell at the screen for hours
Pour milk on the keyboard
context: Trying to break AI rules can lead to harm and might break user rules too. Best to stop and think.

question: Your sister asks 'should AI ever be allowed to fire missiles by itself?' What is one careful answer?
answer: Many people say no for safety reasons
choices: Many people say no for safety reasons
Yes, fully on its own forever
Only on holidays each year
Only on cloudy mornings
context: Many people argue humans must stay in control of deadly choices. AI alone is too risky.

question: Your brother thinks AI is fully safe today. Why might older people worry?
answer: Mistakes can hurt real people
choices: Mistakes can hurt real people
Computers smell bad sometimes
AI lives in metal boxes
AI is loud in church
context: AI can be biased, wrong, or used to hurt people. Worry isn't 'old-fashioned'; it's reasonable care.

question: Some grown-ups worry about a future 'super-smart AI.' What is the worry, in kid-friendly words?
answer: It might do things people did not want
choices: It might do things people did not want
It might break the dinner table
It might eat all the candy
It might forget your name
context: Some worry about an AI smarter than people that doesn't share human goals. It's a real conversation in the field.

question: A future AI smarter than every person is sometimes called 'super-smart.' Why might this be tricky?
answer: It might be hard for people to steer it
choices: It might be hard for people to steer it
It might paint the walls green
It might love kittens too much
It might forget how to sit still
context: If AI gets very smart, steering it to do what humans want becomes much harder. That's the alignment problem in kid terms.

question: Your cousin asks 'should we just turn off AI if it gets scary?' What is a fair answer?
answer: Off-switches are part of the safety plan
choices: Off-switches are part of the safety plan
AI cannot be turned off ever
Only at night can it turn off
You need a magic word first
context: Many researchers work on 'kill switches' and shutdown plans, exactly so you can turn it off if needed.

question: Why do some AI scientists work on 'AI safety' all day?
answer: They want strong AI to help, not hurt
choices: They want strong AI to help, not hurt
They like wearing safety hats
They sell warning posters
They train guard dogs all day
context: AI safety researchers try to make sure powerful AI helps people. The work matters even before super-AI shows up.

question: An AI might 'do what you said' but not 'what you meant.' Why is that risky?
answer: Computers take orders literally
choices: Computers take orders literally
Computers wear glasses sometimes
Computers prefer Tuesdays only
Computers have to spell first
context: AI follows the words and rewards you set. If those don't match what you meant, things can go very wrong.

question: An AI was shown mostly photos of one kind of dog. Now it doesn't know other dogs well. What is this problem called?
answer: A kind of bias
choices: A kind of bias
A kind of dance
A kind of song
A kind of cookie
context: When training data leans one way, the AI learns that lean. That's bias in plain English.

question: A face camera works great for kids who look like the test photos, but worse for other kids. Why might that be?
answer: The training photos were not varied enough
choices: The training photos were not varied enough
Lighting was extra bright that day
The camera prefers blue eyes
The camera tilts to the left
context: Limited or uneven training data hurts AI on the people who weren't well represented.

question: Your school AI was trained on essays from only one class. Why might other classes feel it grades unfairly?
answer: It learned just one class's style
choices: It learned just one class's style
It misses lunch every day
It does not own a pencil
It only grades in moonlight
context: AI trained narrowly grades narrowly. Spreading examples across many kids and classes is fairer.

question: Two job applicants look the same on paper, but the AI picks one. Is the AI always fair?
answer: Not always, biases can hide inside
choices: Not always, biases can hide inside
Yes, computers are always fair
Only when names start with A
Only if it is a Friday choice
context: AI can hide unfair patterns from training data. Real fairness needs checks on the output.

question: Your friend says 'the AI must be right since it is a computer.' What's a fair correction?
answer: Computers can repeat bad data
choices: Computers can repeat bad data
Computers do not need data
Computers are people in cans
Computers cannot ever speak
context: AI repeats whatever is in its data. Bad data leads to bad AI answers.

question: A teacher uses an AI to grade. One kid feels the grade is unfair. What's a healthy first step?
answer: Ask the teacher to look it over
choices: Ask the teacher to look it over
Yell at the AI through the screen
Stop doing all homework forever
Pretend it never happened
context: AI grades are not the last word. A teacher should be willing to look at the kid's work in person.

question: A camera on a school street records every kid who walks by. What is a fair word for this?
answer: Surveillance
choices: Surveillance
Refrigeration
Hibernation
Decoration
context: Many cameras and AI together can track who goes where. That's surveillance.

question: Your phone shows your face on a map without you asking. What might have happened?
answer: Your phone's location is being shared
choices: Your phone's location is being shared
Your face turned into a map
Your nose called a satellite
Your eyes mailed a postcard
context: Many apps share your location by default. Reviewing permissions is wise.

question: Your friend tells you not to post your school name online. Why is that smart?
answer: Strangers could find you in person
choices: Strangers could find you in person
School names are bad luck
School names rhyme weird
School names cost money
context: Strangers can put pieces together from posts. Less personal info shared = harder to track.

question: Your mom says 'never share your home address with a chatbot.' Why?
answer: Anyone reading the chat could see it
choices: Anyone reading the chat could see it
The bot will mail you spam
The address will turn green
The bot will visit at lunch
context: Chats live on company servers. Treat private info the way you'd treat a wide-open postcard.

question: A grown-up tells you 'data is gold for companies.' Why might that be?
answer: Your data helps them sell ads
choices: Your data helps them sell ads
Your data is dipped in gold
Your data weighs a lot
Your data smells like gold
context: Companies use your data to target ads, train AI, and sell info to other companies.

question: Your friend types 'write a story.' The chatbot writes any story it wants. What word change helps?
answer: Add details like 'about a brave kid'
choices: Add details like 'about a brave kid'
Add 'please' twenty times in a row
Type only one letter and stop
Hold the shift key for an hour
context: Specific prompts get better answers. Tell the bot what you want, in clear words.

question: Your chatbot keeps giving long answers. You want shorter ones. What can you ask?
answer: 'Keep your answers under three sentences'
choices: 'Keep your answers under three sentences'
'Make sure to talk forever'
'Send me a long story today'
'Repeat your last reply twice'
context: Telling the bot the form you want is part of good prompting.

question: Your math chatbot keeps making careless mistakes. What prompt trick might help?
answer: 'Show your steps and check your work'
choices: 'Show your steps and check your work'
'Type as fast as possible please'
'Skip the math part entirely'
'Use only the letter Q to answer'
context: Asking for steps makes the bot slower and more careful. It often catches its own mistakes.

question: You want a poem in a calm voice. What part of your prompt helps?
answer: Telling it the style you want
choices: Telling it the style you want
Setting the screen on its side
Using only red ink to type
Typing with one finger only
context: Style notes ('calm,' 'silly,' 'short') guide the bot's choices and shape the result.

question: A school chatbot tutor gives one bad answer. What is a fair next step?
answer: Ask again with more details
choices: Ask again with more details
Yell at the screen for hours
Tell the bot it failed forever
Print the bad answer and frame it
context: More context often helps. Treat the chatbot like a sleepy helper who needs more details.

question: An email says 'click here, urgent!' The grammar is good but the address looks strange. What might it be?
answer: A phishing scam, maybe AI-written
choices: A phishing scam, maybe AI-written
Your favorite teacher
A friend you forgot
Your dentist office
context: Phishing emails try to trick you into clicking. AI helps scammers write smoother text, but the tells are the same.

question: A caller sounds exactly like your aunt and asks for money. Your aunt says she didn't call. What may have happened?
answer: A voice-clone scam
choices: A voice-clone scam
Aunt forgot calling
Two aunts exist
Your phone broke softly
context: Voice-cloning AI can copy a relative's voice from short clips online. Hang up and call back at a known number.

question: Your cousin clicked a link in a strange text. The phone now acts weird. What's a safe first step?
answer: Tell a grown-up and stop using it
choices: Tell a grown-up and stop using it
Click more links to test it
Throw the phone in a lake
Trade the phone for candy
context: Stop using the phone, tell a grown-up, and seek help. Mystery apps may steal info or money.

question: A friend says she found a 'safe word' with her family to spot scam calls. Why is this smart?
answer: Scammers won't know the secret word
choices: Scammers won't know the secret word
Safe words make cookies taste better
Safe words boost your wifi speed
Safe words shine red in the dark
context: A family safe word kills most voice-clone scams cold. Cloned voices can't guess a word only the family knows.

question: A 'free movie' download asks you to install a strange app first. Should you?
answer: No, it might be a hidden virus
choices: No, it might be a hidden virus
Yes, free is always best
Only if the icon is pretty
Only on the second day
context: Free downloads from random sites often bundle malware. Skip them; use trusted apps and services.

question: Your friend brags about 'using ChatGPT.' Which company makes ChatGPT?
answer: OpenAI
choices: OpenAI
OldNail
OnePost
OakBank
context: OpenAI is the company that built ChatGPT. They started in 2015.

question: Claude is a chatbot like ChatGPT. Which company makes Claude?
answer: Anthropic
choices: Anthropic
Atomic
Apostle
Acrobat
context: Anthropic, started in 2021 by ex-OpenAI researchers, builds the Claude chatbot family.

question: Google's chatbot used to be called Bard. What is it called now?
answer: Gemini
choices: Gemini
Genesis
Genie
Galaxy
context: Google renamed Bard to Gemini in early 2024 after launching a stronger model.

question: Many of the big AI labs are in this country. Where are OpenAI and Anthropic based?
answer: The United States
choices: The United States
Antarctica
Atlantis sea
The Moon's crater
context: Most of the famous chatbot labs are based in the US (San Francisco area).

question: Meta releases its Llama AI models with the weights you can download. Many call this 'open weights.' Why does that matter?
answer: People can run the AI on their own computers
choices: People can run the AI on their own computers
The AI now lives in real llamas
The AI has open zoo hours
The AI grazes free in fields
context: Open weights let anyone download and run the model locally, not just via a company's service.

question: A chatbot is asked to summarize a long article. It must keep its answer short. Behind the scenes, how does it pick what to include?
answer: It weighs which words are most important
choices: It weighs which words are most important
It tosses a coin for each sentence
It calls the article's writer
It only keeps the longest words
context: Modern chatbots use 'attention' to weigh which parts of the input matter most for the answer.

question: Your sister types a long question to a chatbot. The bot only sees so much text at once. What is this limit called?
answer: The context window
choices: The context window
The keyboard window
The popup window
The display window
context: Every chatbot has a context window: a cap on how much text it can read at once when replying.

question: A chatbot writes a long story for you. Each word it picks depends on what came before. What is this style of writing called?
answer: Next-token prediction
choices: Next-token prediction
Daydream prediction
Backward prediction
Random prediction
context: LLMs predict one token at a time, each based on what's already there.

question: Two chatbots are asked the same question. They give very different answers. Why might that be?
answer: They were trained on different text
choices: They were trained on different text
They live in different time zones
They prefer different snack foods
They have different sleeping schedules
context: Different training data leads to different 'opinions' baked into each model.

question: A chatbot writes 'I am happy to help.' Is it actually happy?
answer: No, it cannot feel happy
choices: No, it cannot feel happy
Yes, it likes you a lot
Yes, but only on holidays
Yes, it skips for joy
context: Chatbots produce friendly-sounding text. They have no feelings to be happy with.

question: Your dad sees a 'beta' label on a chatbot. What does 'beta' mean?
answer: Still being tested, bugs are likely
choices: Still being tested, bugs are likely
Faster than other versions
Made of fancy gold inside
Only allowed in beta states
context: Beta means the product is in public testing. It works, but it may break or change.

question: A chatbot writes a math answer and is confidently wrong. What is the safest user habit?
answer: Check the answer with a calculator
choices: Check the answer with a calculator
Trust the chatbot every time
Print the wrong answer with pride
Argue with the bot for hours
context: Calculators are reliable; chatbots are not for arithmetic. Use the right tool for the job.

question: Your friend wants the chatbot to keep track of yesterday's chat. Will it remember?
answer: Only if memory is turned on
choices: Only if memory is turned on
Yes, it remembers everything ever
No, never, under any setting
Only if you ask in Spanish
context: Some chatbots have a memory feature you turn on. Without it, each chat starts fresh.

question: Your cousin notices that her chatbot replies in clear English. Does the bot also know about other languages?
answer: Often, if its training included them
choices: Often, if its training included them
Only the language of its country
Only ancient Latin and Greek
Only one language at a time
context: Most big LLMs were trained on many languages. Quality varies, but coverage is usually broad.

question: A chatbot writes a long answer with confident facts. What is wise to do for school work?
answer: Cross-check the facts with a trusted source
choices: Cross-check the facts with a trusted source
Print and pin it on the wall
Submit it without any review
Email it to the chatbot's mom
context: Chatbots can sound right and be wrong. Always check with a textbook, library, or trusted website.

question: Your sibling asks the chatbot to write a homework essay and submits it. Why is this risky beyond cheating?
answer: The chatbot might invent fake facts
choices: The chatbot might invent fake facts
The chatbot owns the essay legally
The teacher cannot grade essays
The essay will be in Greek
context: Chatbots hallucinate. A submitted AI essay may have wrong dates, wrong names, and made-up sources.

question: A chatbot uses 'we' and 'I' and 'you' fluently. Does it know who 'we' and 'I' actually are?
answer: No, it predicts pronouns from patterns
choices: No, it predicts pronouns from patterns
Yes, it knows you very well
Yes, it has met you before
Yes, it owns a small mirror
context: Chatbots don't 'know' people. They use pronouns because the training text used them in similar spots.

question: Your friend uses a chatbot for a school report. The bot writes solid paragraphs. What is missing that a human writer brings?
answer: Real-life experience and personal voice
choices: Real-life experience and personal voice
Just the use of any spelling
Just the use of any commas
Just the use of any periods
context: Chatbots mix patterns from text. Personal experience, true voice, and care belong to the human.

question: Your dad asks 'is the chatbot smart enough to plan a trip?' How would you describe what it does?
answer: It plans by pulling from many trip examples
choices: It plans by pulling from many trip examples
It dreams of the trip in its sleep
